Deep time also records episodes that resemble, in kind if not in scale or speed, the current experiment. During the Palaeocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum, about 56 million years ago, a massive release of carbon, probably several thousand gigatonnes over a few thousand years, warmed the planet by several degrees, acidified the oceans, and dissolved carbonate sediments on the sea floor. It took the cycle well over a hundred thousand years to recover, as silicate weathering slowly consumed the excess carbon. This event is studied closely because it is the closest natural analogue to modern carbon release, and its recovery timescale illustrates how slowly the geological cycle heals such a disturbance.

Comparing that ancient event with today sharpens the lesson. Estimates suggest the carbon released during the Palaeocene-Eocene event entered the atmosphere over thousands of years, whereas the comparable modern release is happening over roughly a century, at least ten times faster and possibly much more. The rate matters as much as the total, because the fast reservoirs and ecosystems can adjust to gradual change but are stressed by abrupt change. The deep-time record therefore delivers two messages at once. It shows that the carbon cycle is resilient over the very long run, always eventually returning to balance through weathering and burial. And it shows that this resilience operates on timescales of tens to hundreds of thousands of years, far beyond human planning horizons, so that a perturbation delivered in a single century is, from the standpoint of any human society, effectively irreversible.

guides.title: Climate Feedback Loops
guides.summary: How the Earth system amplifies or damps a change in its energy balance: the physics and arithmetic of feedbacks, each major loop from water vapour and clouds to ice, permafrost and ocean circulation, the evidence behind them, and what is genuinely known versus still contested.

sections.heading: What a Feedback Is, and Why the Climate Runs on Them
sections.body: A feedback is any process by which the output of a system loops back to change its own input. If a nudge to a system provokes a response that reinforces the nudge, the feedback is positive and the system amplifies disturbances. If the response opposes the nudge, the feedback is negative and the system damps them. The words are unfortunate, because positive sounds good and negative sounds bad, whereas in climate the negative feedbacks are the ones keeping the planet habitable and the positive ones are the reason a modest change in atmospheric composition can produce a large change in temperature. The distinction that makes the whole subject tractable is between a forcing and a feedback. A forcing is an imposed change in the planet's energy budget that does not itself depend on the resulting temperature: the sun brightening, a volcano injecting sulfate aerosol into the stratosphere, humans burning coal and adding carbon dioxide. A feedback is a change that occurs because the temperature changed, and which then alters the energy budget further. Water vapour is the textbook example. Nobody emits enough water vapour to matter, because the atmosphere removes it within about nine days; its concentration is set almost entirely by temperature. So water vapour is not a forcing but a feedback, and a powerful one. Carbon dioxide, with a residence time in the coupled ocean-atmosphere system of centuries to millennia, behaves in the opposite way: on human timescales it is a forcing, though across ice ages it acted as a feedback on orbital changes. The reason feedbacks dominate the climate problem is arithmetic. Doubling carbon dioxide from its pre-industrial 278 parts per million imposes a forcing of roughly 3.9 watts per square metre. If the planet simply warmed until it radiated that much extra energy back to space, with nothing else changing, the surface would warm by only about 1.2 degrees Celsius. The best estimate of what actually happens is about 3 degrees. Everything between 1.2 and 3 is feedback — the planet's own response to its own warming — and it is where essentially all of the scientific difficulty, and all of the remaining uncertainty about how bad the century ahead will be, is concentrated. Feedbacks also operate on wildly different timescales, which is why a single number for climate sensitivity is always an abstraction. Water vapour adjusts in days, clouds in days to weeks, sea ice over years to decades, the ocean's deep heat uptake over centuries, ice sheets and the carbon cycle over centuries to many millennia. A useful description of the climate is therefore not one loop but a nested hierarchy of them, each with its own gain and its own clock.

sections.heading: The Arithmetic of Feedback: Forcing, Sensitivity and Gain
sections.body: The standard framework treats the top-of-atmosphere energy imbalance as a linear function of surface temperature. Write N for the net downward imbalance in watts per square metre, F for the imposed forcing, and delta T for the change in global mean surface temperature. Then N equals F plus lambda times delta T, where lambda is the net feedback parameter, in watts per square metre per degree. Because a warmer planet radiates more, lambda is negative for a stable climate. At equilibrium the imbalance has vanished, N equals zero, and the equilibrium warming is minus F divided by lambda. Individual feedbacks are assumed to add, so lambda is the sum of a Planck term and the others. The Sixth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, published in 2021, assessed these in watts per square metre per degree as follows: Planck about minus 3.22; water vapour plus 1.30; lapse rate minus 0.50; surface albedo plus 0.35; clouds plus 0.42; and a small biogeophysical term near zero. The sum is about minus 1.16, with an assessed range from about minus 1.81 to minus 0.51. Dividing a 3.9 watt forcing by 1.16 gives about 3.4 degrees, and the assessed best estimate of equilibrium climate sensitivity is 3 degrees, with a likely range of 2.5 to 4 and a very likely range of 2 to 5. Two features of this arithmetic deserve emphasis. First, sensitivity depends on one over the net feedback, so uncertainty is strongly asymmetric. Shifting lambda from minus 1.2 to minus 1.0 raises the warming from 3.3 to 3.9 degrees, whereas shifting it to minus 1.4 lowers it only to 2.8. As the net feedback approaches zero the response diverges, which is why the upper tail of every sensitivity estimate is long. Second, the framework is a linearisation, assuming feedbacks are proportional to global mean temperature and independent of one another. Two other quantities are used because they are more directly relevant to policy. The transient climate response is the warming at the moment of carbon dioxide doubling under a one per cent per year increase, assessed at about 1.8 degrees; it is smaller than equilibrium sensitivity because the deep ocean is still absorbing heat. The transient climate response to cumulative emissions expresses warming per trillion tonnes of carbon emitted, assessed at roughly 1.65 degrees, and its near-linearity is the reason a carbon budget is a coherent concept at all. That near-linearity is itself the accidental product of two effects pulling opposite ways: the logarithmic weakening of carbon dioxide's forcing, and the declining efficiency of the sinks. It is convenient rather than fundamental. A related concept, the feedback gain, expresses the same idea dimensionlessly. Define g as the sum of the non-Planck feedbacks divided by the magnitude of the Planck term. With amplifying feedbacks near 2 and a Planck term near 3.2, g is about 0.64, and the amplification factor is one divided by one minus g, roughly 2.8. Warming of 1.2 degrees becomes about 3.3. The formula makes the upper tail vivid: at a gain of 0.8 the amplification is five, and at 0.9 it is ten.

sections.heading: The Planck Response: The Feedback That Keeps Earth Stable
sections.body: Before any of the interesting feedbacks operate, there is one that always acts and always opposes change. Every object radiates energy at a rate that rises steeply with its temperature. The Stefan-Boltzmann law, established by Josef Stefan in 1879 and derived thermodynamically by Ludwig Boltzmann in 1884, states that the emitted flux is proportional to the fourth power of absolute temperature, with a constant of 5.67 times ten to the minus eight watts per square metre per kelvin to the fourth. Warm the planet and it sheds heat faster; cool it and it sheds heat more slowly. This is the Planck response, and it is the reason Earth has a stable climate at all rather than wandering immediately to one extreme. Its magnitude follows from differentiating that law. Earth radiates to space at an effective temperature near 255 kelvin, and four times the Stefan-Boltzmann constant times 255 cubed gives about 3.8 watts per square metre per kelvin. Detailed radiative calculations that account for the vertical structure of the atmosphere and the fact that different wavelengths escape from different altitudes yield a slightly smaller figure, about 3.2 watts per square metre per degree of surface warming. That single number sets the scale for everything else: it is the yardstick against which every other feedback is measured, and any feedback smaller than a few tenths of a watt per square metre per degree is a detail. Dividing the doubled-carbon-dioxide forcing by the Planck response gives what is sometimes called the no-feedback or blackbody sensitivity, about 1.2 degrees. This figure is not controversial in any quarter; it follows from radiative physics that has been verified in the laboratory and by satellite spectrometers observing the actual outgoing spectrum. Svante Arrhenius arrived at a broadly comparable framework in 1896, calculating by hand from Samuel Langley's lunar infrared measurements that halving or doubling carbon dioxide would change surface temperature by several degrees. His number was too high, his method crude, and he expected the change would take three thousand years, but the physical logic was right. Because the Planck response is always present and always stabilising, the interesting question is never whether a feedback is positive but whether the sum of the positive ones can outweigh it. If the total of the amplifying feedbacks exceeded 3.2 watts per square metre per degree, the net lambda would become positive and warming would run away without limit until some new physics intervened. The observed stability of Earth's climate through hundreds of millions of years of large forcings is itself strong evidence that this threshold has not been crossed, and modern estimates put the sum of amplifying feedbacks near 2 watts per square metre per degree — large, but comfortably short of runaway.

sections.heading: Water Vapour: The Largest Amplifier
sections.body: Water vapour is the strongest greenhouse gas in Earth's atmosphere, responsible for roughly half of the total greenhouse effect, with clouds contributing about a quarter and carbon dioxide about a fifth. It is also the single largest amplifying feedback in the climate system, contributing about plus 1.3 watts per square metre per degree — enough on its own to roughly double the no-feedback warming. The mechanism rests on a piece of nineteenth-century thermodynamics. The Clausius-Clapeyron relation, derived from the equality of chemical potential between liquid and vapour, states that the saturation vapour pressure of water rises roughly exponentially with temperature, by about 7 per cent per degree Celsius near current surface conditions. Warm air can simply hold more moisture. Observations from radiosondes, satellite microwave sounders and ground-based instruments confirm that as the world has warmed, relative humidity has stayed approximately constant while absolute humidity has risen close to the rate Clausius-Clapeyron predicts, at about 7 per cent per degree in the lower troposphere. More water vapour absorbs more outgoing infrared radiation, which warms the surface further, which permits still more water vapour: a classic amplifying loop. Constant relative humidity is an emergent result rather than an assumption. It arises because evaporation and precipitation are both fast, and because the humidity of the free troposphere is largely set by the temperature at which air last condensed out its moisture during ascent. The upper troposphere matters disproportionately, because radiation escapes to space from around 8 to 12 kilometres altitude, where the air is cold and dry and where adding a little vapour changes the emission height a great deal. Early scepticism, notably from Richard Lindzen in the 1990s, proposed that deeper convection might dry the upper troposphere and cancel the effect. Satellite measurements over subsequent decades have not supported that, and upper-tropospheric moistening is now directly observed. There is a hard ceiling on the loop's strength, which is why it does not run away. Each successive increment of water vapour adds less absorption than the last, because the strongest absorption bands become saturated and further absorption occurs only in the weaker wings. Mathematically, the feedback gain is well below one, so the geometric series it generates converges. On a hotter planet the story changes: if the surface exceeds roughly 340 kelvin the atmosphere can reach a state where increasing vapour no longer increases the escaping radiation at all, the so-called Simpson-Nakajima limit, and a true runaway greenhouse follows. That is thought to have happened on Venus. Careful calculations, including work by Colin Goldblatt and colleagues in 2012, indicate that Earth cannot reach that state by burning fossil fuels; the solar constant is not yet high enough. The water vapour feedback is very large, well constrained, and finite.

sections.heading: The Lapse-Rate Feedback and Why It Cancels Part of the Water Vapour Loop
sections.body: The lapse rate is the rate at which temperature falls with altitude, on average about 6.5 degrees per kilometre in the troposphere. It matters because the planet loses heat to space from altitude, not from the ground. If the upper troposphere warms more than the surface, the emitting layers become warmer than the surface change alone would suggest, radiation to space increases faster, and the warming is damped. That is the lapse-rate feedback, and globally it is negative, at about minus 0.5 watts per square metre per degree. The physics behind it is moist convection. Rising air cools as it expands, but condensing water vapour releases latent heat that partly offsets the cooling, so a moist atmosphere has a shallower lapse rate than a dry one. In the tropics the vertical temperature profile is held close to a moist adiabat by vigorous deep convection, and warming a moist adiabat warms the upper troposphere more than the surface — by roughly a factor of two at 10 kilometres. This produces the so-called tropical upper-tropospheric hot spot, which is a robust prediction of basic thermodynamics rather than a model artefact, though detecting it in noisy radiosonde records has been contentious for years and observational agreement is still imperfect. In polar regions the sign reverses. The high-latitude atmosphere is stably stratified, with strong surface inversions in winter, and convection is weak. Warming there is concentrated near the surface and barely reaches the upper troposphere, so the emitting layers warm less than the surface, radiation increases less, and the local lapse-rate feedback is positive. This bottom-heavy warming structure is now recognised as one of the main contributors to Arctic amplification, alongside the loss of reflective ice, and analyses since about 2014 have argued it may be as important as the albedo effect itself. The crucial point for the global picture is that the lapse-rate and water-vapour feedbacks are physically linked and strongly anti-correlated across models. A model that moistens the upper troposphere strongly also warms it strongly, gaining a larger positive water-vapour feedback and a larger negative lapse-rate feedback at the same time. Consequently their sum is far better constrained than either term separately: the combined water-vapour-plus-lapse-rate feedback is assessed at about plus 0.8 watts per square metre per degree, with an uncertainty of only about plus or minus 0.24. Quoting either number in isolation exaggerates how uncertain this part of the system is, and treating them as independent contributors is a common error in popular summaries. There is a further subtlety with practical consequences. Because the polar lapse-rate feedback is positive while the tropical one is negative, the global average depends on where the warming happens. This is one strand of what is now called the pattern effect: the feedback inferred from the last 150 years, whose warming has been concentrated in particular ocean regions, may be more negative than the feedback that applies once warming spreads. It is one reason sensitivity estimates derived purely from the historical record came out lower than those from models and palaeoclimate.

sections.heading: Clouds: The Largest Remaining Uncertainty
sections.body: Clouds do two opposing things. They reflect incoming sunlight back to space, cooling the planet, and they absorb and re-emit outgoing infrared radiation, warming it. In the present climate the reflective effect wins overall: clouds cool Earth by a net of roughly 20 watts per square metre, cooling by about 45 through reflection and warming by about 25 through the greenhouse effect. The feedback question is not whether clouds cool, but how that balance shifts as the planet warms — and the answer depends delicately on cloud type, altitude, thickness and geography. Height is the dominant control on the infrared side. A high, cold cirrus cloud radiates to space at a very low temperature and therefore emits little, trapping heat efficiently; a low stratocumulus deck radiates at nearly the surface temperature and traps almost nothing while reflecting a great deal of sunlight. As the atmosphere warms and deepens, high cloud tops rise to stay at roughly the same temperature — the fixed anvil temperature hypothesis proposed by Dennis Hartmann and Marc Larson in 2002, since refined into the proportionately higher anvil temperature idea — so they remain cold while the surface below warms, and the greenhouse trapping grows. That is a positive feedback with a fairly solid theoretical basis. The larger and more contested term is low marine cloud, particularly the vast stratocumulus sheets over the cool eastern subtropical oceans off California, Peru and Namibia. These decks reflect strongly and cover a substantial fraction of the tropics. Warming tends to thin and break them up, partly by strengthening the trade inversion, partly by increasing the vertical humidity contrast that drives entrainment of dry air from above. Less low cloud means more absorbed sunlight, which is a positive feedback. Large-eddy simulations, which resolve individual cloud-scale turbulence over small domains, consistently find such thinning; one much-discussed 2019 study by Tapio Schneider and colleagues found that at very high carbon dioxide, above about 1,200 parts per million, stratocumulus decks could break up altogether, causing several degrees of abrupt additional warming, though this remains a single idealised result rather than an established prediction. The overall assessed cloud feedback is now positive, about plus 0.42 watts per square metre per degree, with a range that still spans roughly minus 0.10 to plus 0.94. That is the largest single uncertainty in climate sensitivity. Confidence in the positive sign has nevertheless risen markedly since 2015, driven less by global models — whose grids of 25 to 100 kilometres cannot resolve clouds at all and must parameterise them — than by process-level modelling, satellite records of cloud-controlling factors, and observed responses to natural variability. Honest reporting requires saying both things: the sign is now reasonably secure, and the magnitude is not.

sections.heading: Ice, Snow and the Albedo Feedback
sections.body: Albedo is the fraction of incoming sunlight a surface reflects. Fresh snow reflects 0.8 to 0.9 of the light falling on it; old melting snow perhaps 0.5; bare sea ice about 0.5 to 0.7; melt ponds on ice around 0.2 to 0.4; and open ocean only about 0.06, absorbing more than nine tenths of the sunlight it receives. Replacing a white surface with a dark one at high latitude therefore represents an enormous local change in absorbed energy, and that is the ice-albedo feedback: warming melts ice, the exposed surface absorbs more sunlight, and the region warms further, melting more ice. Globally the surface albedo feedback is assessed at about plus 0.35 watts per square metre per degree, the third largest amplifier after water vapour and clouds. It is smaller than the local effect suggests because ice-covered regions are a modest fraction of the planet and receive sunlight at glancing angles for part of the year, and because during the polar winter, when Arctic sea ice loss is now greatest, there is no sunlight at all to absorb. Its observed signature is Arctic amplification. Since satellite records began in 1979 the Arctic has warmed roughly three to four times faster than the global mean; a 2022 analysis by Mika Rantanen and colleagues put the ratio near 3.8 for the region north of 66 degrees. September Arctic sea ice extent has declined by roughly 12 to 13 per cent per decade, and the multi-year ice that once dominated has been largely replaced by thinner first-year ice, which melts out more readily and so ratchets the loss. Amplification is not solely albedo; the positive polar lapse-rate feedback, increased poleward heat and moisture transport, and changes in cloud cover all contribute, and disentangling their shares remains an active question. Antarctica behaves quite differently and the contrast is instructive. The Southern Ocean surrounds the continent with a vast reservoir of water that mixes heat downward, the circumpolar winds isolate it, and Antarctic sea ice showed no clear decline and even modest growth until an abrupt drop from 2016 onward whose causes are still debated. This asymmetry is a useful reminder that a feedback's expression depends on the geography and circulation it operates within, not only on its physics. On long timescales the ice-albedo loop can be genuinely runaway. During the Cryogenian period, roughly 717 to 635 million years ago, ice appears to have advanced to low latitudes in at least two episodes, the Snowball Earth events, in which the albedo feedback ran to completion and only the slow accumulation of volcanic carbon dioxide over millions of years eventually broke the state. Nothing comparable is possible in the present warming direction, because Earth simply lacks enough ice to matter: melting every glacier and ice sheet would change global albedo far less than a snowball transition did, and the feedback shuts off entirely once the ice is gone.

sections.heading: The Carbon Cycle as a Feedback
sections.body: Roughly half of every tonne of carbon dioxide humans emit does not stay in the atmosphere. Of about 10 to 11 billion tonnes of carbon released each year from fossil fuels and land use in the early 2020s, the ocean absorbs about a quarter and land ecosystems about a third, leaving an airborne fraction near 45 per cent. These sinks are not fixed pipes; they respond to both carbon dioxide concentration and to temperature, and those two responses are feedbacks of opposite sign. The concentration-carbon feedback is negative and helpful. Higher atmospheric carbon dioxide pushes more gas into the ocean by simple partial-pressure difference, and it stimulates plant photosynthesis, the carbon dioxide fertilisation effect, which satellite records of vegetation greenness support at the global scale even as its magnitude at the level of individual ecosystems is contested and appears to be saturating where nitrogen or phosphorus is limiting. The climate-carbon feedback is positive and harmful. Warmer water holds less dissolved gas, warmer soils respire stored organic carbon faster — soil respiration roughly doubles for every 10 degrees of warming, the familiar Q10 relation — and warmer, drier conditions reduce plant uptake and increase fire. The ocean's chemistry imposes an additional and underappreciated limit. Dissolved carbon dioxide reacts with water and carbonate to form bicarbonate, and it is that reaction, not simple physical solubility, that gives the ocean its enormous capacity. But as more carbon enters, the carbonate ion pool is drawn down and the buffering weakens. The Revelle factor, named for Roger Revelle who with Hans Suess identified the problem in 1957, expresses this: it is currently around 10 in surface waters, meaning a 10 per cent rise in dissolved inorganic carbon requires a 100 per cent rise in carbon dioxide partial pressure. The factor is rising as the ocean acidifies, so each additional tonne is absorbed less readily. Revelle's paper contained the memorable observation that humanity was carrying out a large-scale geophysical experiment that could not be repeated. Coupled carbon-cycle model comparisons since the C4MIP project of 2006 consistently find that the positive climate-carbon feedback outweighs nothing but is outweighed by the concentration effect for now, so the sinks continue to grow in absolute terms while shrinking as a fraction of emissions. The spread between models is large, equivalent to a few tens of parts per million to well over a hundred by 2100, and it is one of the main reasons the same emissions scenario produces different concentrations in different Earth system models. There is emerging observational evidence that the land sink is becoming more variable and more vulnerable to drought years, which is a signal worth watching closely. The practical implication is that emissions and concentrations are not the same problem. A tonne removed from the atmosphere by direct capture is only partly a tonne of benefit, because the ocean and land respond by giving some carbon back as the concentration falls — the same feedback in reverse. Roughly half of any removal is offset this way over decades, a counter-intuitive result and a strong argument for avoiding emissions rather than planning to reverse them.

sections.heading: Permafrost and Frozen Carbon
sections.body: Permafrost is ground that has remained at or below zero degrees Celsius for at least two consecutive years. It underlies roughly 15 per cent of the exposed land area of the northern hemisphere, extending in places to depths of several hundred metres, and it contains an enormous store of organic carbon — plant and animal material frozen before it could decompose, accumulated over tens of thousands of years. The northern permafrost region is estimated to hold about 1,400 to 1,600 billion tonnes of carbon in the upper three metres and in deeper deposits such as the Pleistocene yedoma silts of Siberia and Alaska. That is roughly twice the carbon currently in the atmosphere, and about four times what humans have emitted in the industrial era. The feedback mechanism is straightforward. Warming deepens the active layer, the seasonally thawed surface soil, and eventually thaws permafrost outright. Microbes then get access to organic matter that has been unavailable for millennia and respire it, producing carbon dioxide where oxygen is available and methane where the ground is waterlogged. Both gases warm the atmosphere, deepening the thaw. Because methane's warming effect per molecule is far larger over decadal timescales — its 100-year global warming potential is about 27 to 30 for biogenic sources — the wet-versus-dry split matters disproportionately, and it is one of the harder things to project. Estimates of the size of the feedback have converged somewhat but remain wide. The 2021 IPCC assessment gave a permafrost carbon feedback of roughly 18 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide-equivalent released per degree of global warming, with a range of about 3 to 41, corresponding to an additional warming of perhaps 0.04 to 0.11 degrees by 2100 under moderate scenarios and more under high ones. Most model estimates of the century-scale contribution fall in the range of a few tenths of a degree. This is substantial — comparable to the emissions of a large industrialised nation, and irreversible on human timescales — but it is not the civilisation-ending bomb sometimes described in popular accounts. Two genuine uncertainties keep the range wide. The first is abrupt thaw: thermokarst, in which ice-rich ground collapses to form lakes and gullies, can expose deep carbon far faster than gradual warming of the soil column, and it affects perhaps 20 per cent of the permafrost region while potentially contributing a disproportionate share of emissions. Most large-scale models represent only gradual thaw. The second is the offsetting effect of vegetation: warmer Arctic summers lengthen the growing season and shrubs advance northward, taking up carbon, which partly compensates in the early decades before respiration losses dominate. A third consideration is that the release is effectively one-way. Refreezing the ground would take centuries of sustained cooling, and the carbon respired cannot be put back into the frozen state that held it. Permafrost carbon therefore behaves less like a reversible feedback and more like a slow, irrevocable addition to the human emissions total, which is why it is normally subtracted from the remaining carbon budget rather than modelled as a variable that policy could later recover.

sections.heading: Methane and the Short-Lived Amplifiers
sections.body: Methane is the second most important greenhouse gas from human activity, and it participates in several feedbacks of its own. Its atmospheric concentration has risen from about 720 parts per billion before industrialisation to over 1,930 today, and although it is present at a fraction of carbon dioxide's concentration, each molecule absorbs far more strongly in a spectral window where the atmosphere is otherwise relatively transparent. Its 100-year global warming potential is about 27 to 30, and its 20-year potential is over 80, reflecting a short atmospheric lifetime of roughly 9 to 12 years. The natural sources are mostly biological and temperature-sensitive. Wetlands are the largest, releasing methane from anaerobic decomposition in waterlogged soils, and their emissions rise with both temperature and rainfall. A warmer, wetter tropics therefore emits more methane, a positive feedback whose magnitude models estimate at a few tens of parts per billion per degree, though wetland extent is one of the poorest-constrained quantities in the entire carbon cycle. The unusually rapid growth in atmospheric methane since 2007, and its sharp acceleration around 2020, has been attributed by isotopic evidence — a shift toward lighter carbon-13 — primarily to biological rather than fossil sources, which raises the uncomfortable possibility that a wetland feedback is already engaging. That interpretation is actively debated, and reduced destruction of methane is an alternative explanation. The sink is itself a feedback. Methane is destroyed mainly by reaction with the hydroxyl radical, the atmosphere's principal cleansing agent, produced when ultraviolet light splits ozone in the presence of water vapour. Because methane consumes hydroxyl as it is destroyed, a large methane increase depletes its own sink and lengthens its own lifetime — a positive chemical feedback that adds roughly a third again to methane's direct effect and is included in its stated warming potential. Marine methane clathrates deserve careful and sceptical treatment because they are the subject of the most exaggerated claims in the field. These are ice-like solids in which methane is caged in a water lattice, stable at the low temperatures and high pressures of continental margin sediments, holding perhaps 1,500 to 2,000 billion tonnes of carbon. The clathrate gun hypothesis proposed that warming could destabilise them catastrophically. Subsequent work has substantially weakened it. Most clathrate lies hundreds of metres below the seafloor, and heat takes centuries to millennia to diffuse there; methane released at depth is largely oxidised by microbes in the sediment and water column before reaching the surface; and observed seabed seeps, including those off Svalbard, have not produced detectable atmospheric anomalies. The current assessment is that a large abrupt clathrate release this century is very unlikely, while a slow release over millennia remains plausible.

sections.heading: Vegetation, Fire and Land-Surface Feedbacks
sections.body: The land surface participates in the climate through more than carbon. Vegetation alters albedo, roughness and the partitioning of energy between heating the air and evaporating water, and each of these gives rise to feedbacks that can differ in sign from region to region. The clearest is the boreal darkening feedback. Snow-covered tundra is highly reflective; a conifer forest, whose dark canopy protrudes above the snow, is not. As warming lets the treeline advance northward, the surface darkens, absorbs more sunlight, and warms further. Palaeoclimate reconstructions of the mid-Holocene, around six thousand years ago, indicate that this taiga-tundra feedback amplified the orbitally driven high-latitude warming appreciably. It works in reverse too, and is thought to have helped push the system into glacial states. Notably, the biogeophysical warming from boreal forest expansion can exceed the biogeochemical cooling from the carbon those trees store, which complicates simple assumptions that planting trees everywhere cools the planet; in the tropics, by contrast, forests cool strongly through evaporation and cloud formation, and the case for protecting them is unambiguous. Fire is a fast, visible feedback that is becoming more important. Warmer, drier conditions increase the length of the fire season and the flammability of fuel; fire releases stored carbon, destroys the insulating moss layer that protects permafrost, and deposits soot on snow and ice, darkening it. The boreal and Arctic fires of recent years, including the extraordinary Canadian season of 2023 that released on the order of half a billion tonnes of carbon, are within the range of what models expect but at the severe end. Peat fires are particularly consequential because peatlands store carbon accumulated over thousands of years and can smoulder underground for months. Drought-driven forest dieback is the most discussed and least resolved land feedback. The Hadley Centre model of 2000 famously projected a collapse of the Amazon rainforest under high warming, converting a carbon sink into a source. Most subsequent models produce far less dramatic outcomes, and the original result depended on a particularly dry rainfall projection for the region. Observationally, parts of the south-eastern Amazon have already flipped to being a net carbon source, driven jointly by deforestation, fire and drought. The honest statement is that large-scale Amazon dieback is plausible and would be consequential, that deforestation and climate act together to bring it closer, and that its threshold and likelihood are genuinely not known. The mechanism that makes the Amazon a candidate for a self-reinforcing collapse is moisture recycling. Air arriving from the Atlantic delivers rainfall, much of which is returned to the atmosphere by transpiration and falls again further inland, so that a given water molecule may be recycled five or six times on its journey west. Estimates suggest something like a quarter to a third of Amazon rainfall originates from the forest itself. Remove enough forest and the recycling weakens, the dry season lengthens, and the remaining forest becomes less able to survive it — a positive feedback internal to the ecosystem rather than to the global energy budget.

sections.heading: Ocean Circulation and Heat Uptake
sections.body: The ocean is where more than 90 per cent of the extra energy trapped by greenhouse gases has gone, and its behaviour governs both how fast the surface warms and how the warming is distributed. Its heat uptake acts like a negative feedback on the transient response: energy carried into the deep water is energy not warming the atmosphere, which is why the transient climate response is roughly 40 per cent smaller than the equilibrium sensitivity, and why warming would continue for centuries even if emissions stopped abruptly. The Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation, or AMOC, is the most closely watched circulation feature. Warm, salty surface water flows north in the Gulf Stream and its extension, gives up heat to the atmosphere over the North Atlantic, becomes dense enough to sink in the Labrador and Nordic Seas, and returns south at depth. The overturning transports something like 17 sverdrups, that is 17 million cubic metres per second, and carries roughly a petawatt of heat northward, which is why north-west Europe is milder than equivalent latitudes in North America. Its feedback structure was captured in a famously simple model by Henry Stommel in 1961. The circulation is driven by density, which depends on both temperature and salinity, and these compete. Warming and freshening of the northern surface — from a warmer atmosphere, from increased rainfall, and from Greenland meltwater — both reduce density and weaken the sinking. A weaker circulation carries less salt northward, which freshens the north further and weakens it more. That is the salt-advection feedback, and it is positive, which is why the system can in principle have two stable states and can jump between them. The abrupt Dansgaard-Oeschger events recorded in Greenland ice cores, in which temperatures rose by 8 to 15 degrees within decades, are widely interpreted as such transitions. Assessment is deliberately cautious. Observations from the RAPID array across 26 degrees north since 2004 show large variability and a possible modest decline, but the record is short relative to natural fluctuations. Proxy reconstructions suggest the circulation is weaker now than at any time in the past millennium, though these are indirect. The IPCC assessed with medium confidence that AMOC will weaken during this century, and with medium confidence that it will not collapse abruptly before 2100, while explicitly acknowledging low confidence in the model basis for that reassurance. Several papers since 2023 have argued for earlier collapse; they rely on statistical early-warning signals in indirect data and remain contested. Two further points are worth carrying away. First, a weakening AMOC produces a distinctive regional signature — a cold blob in the subpolar North Atlantic, which has in fact been observed in an ocean that otherwise warmed almost everywhere. Whether it is a fingerprint of slowdown or a product of natural variability and aerosol history is exactly the open question. Second, the pattern of ocean heat uptake feeds back on the radiative feedbacks themselves: where the ocean holds the surface cool, low cloud persists and the local feedback is strongly negative, so as those regions warm the damping weakens and effective sensitivity rises slowly over centuries.

sections.heading: Ice Sheets and the Slow Feedbacks
sections.body: Greenland and Antarctica hold enough ice to raise global sea level by about 7.4 and 58 metres respectively, and they respond to warming through several feedbacks that act over centuries to millennia. These are excluded from the standard definition of climate sensitivity, which holds ice sheets fixed, and their inclusion gives the larger Earth system sensitivity, estimated from palaeoclimate at perhaps 5 to 8 degrees per carbon dioxide doubling. Greenland's dominant loop is the surface elevation feedback. The ice sheet is up to 3 kilometres thick, and its summit is cold largely because it is high. As the surface melts and the sheet thins, the exposed surface sits at a lower and therefore warmer elevation, which increases melting further. With the atmospheric lapse rate near 6.5 degrees per kilometre, losing 500 metres of thickness warms the surface by roughly 3 degrees, quite independently of any change in the climate around it. Melt-albedo effects compound this: melting darkens snow, exposes bare ice, and concentrates dust, algae and soot, and the resulting biological darkening of the Greenland ablation zone has measurably accelerated loss since the 2000s. Model studies suggest a threshold somewhere in the range of 1.5 to 3 degrees of global warming beyond which the sheet commits to substantial or eventual complete loss over one to several millennia, though the threshold value is genuinely uncertain and the timescale is long. West Antarctica has a different and more alarming mechanism. Much of it is a marine ice sheet, resting on bedrock far below sea level, and in many places that bedrock slopes downward inland. Marine ice sheet instability, described by Johannes Weertman in 1974 and formalised by Christian Schoof in 2007, follows from the fact that the ice flux across the grounding line — the boundary where the sheet begins to float — rises steeply with ice thickness. On a retrograde bed, retreat moves the grounding line into thicker ice, which discharges faster, which drives further retreat. Once begun, the process needs no further warming to continue. Observations of the Amundsen Sea sector, particularly Thwaites and Pine Island glaciers, show grounding-line retreat, thinning, and warm circumpolar deep water reaching the ice shelf cavities; several analyses since 2014 have argued that retreat there may already be underway. A further proposed mechanism, marine ice cliff instability, holds that once buttressing ice shelves are removed, exposed ice cliffs above roughly 90 metres would fail structurally and collapse serially. Introduced into sea-level projections by Robert DeConto and David Pollard in 2016, it produced dramatic results, and subsequent work has substantially qualified it. It is best described as physically plausible, poorly constrained, not currently observed at scale, and excluded from central projections while remaining a reason the high end cannot be dismissed.

sections.heading: Tipping Points, Thresholds and Hysteresis
sections.body: A tipping point is a threshold beyond which a self-reinforcing feedback carries a system to a qualitatively different state, which then persists even if the original forcing is removed. The technical description is a bifurcation in a system with multiple stable equilibria, and the practical signature is hysteresis: the path back is not the path in. If an ice sheet collapses at 2 degrees of warming, returning to 1.5 does not rebuild it, because rebuilding requires the much colder conditions under which it originally grew. That asymmetry, more than the abruptness, is what makes tipping points consequential for policy. The concept entered mainstream climate discussion through a 2008 paper by Timothy Lenton and colleagues, which identified a set of tipping elements — large-scale components with plausible threshold behaviour. An updated assessment led by David Armstrong McKay in 2022 catalogued sixteen, of which several were judged possibly within reach at 1.1 to 1.5 degrees of warming: the Greenland and West Antarctic ice sheets, low-latitude coral reefs, abrupt permafrost thaw, and the Labrador Sea convection cell. Others, including AMOC collapse, Amazon dieback and boreal forest shifts, were placed at higher thresholds with wider ranges. Several honest caveats belong beside those numbers. The thresholds carry very large uncertainties, often spanning several degrees, and mostly derive from model behaviour rather than observed transitions. The word tipping suggests speed, but the transitions differ enormously in pace: coral reef loss can follow a single marine heatwave within years, while ice sheet disintegration unfolds over centuries even once committed. And the evidence that any element possesses a true bifurcation, rather than merely a strong nonlinear response, is stronger for some than others. The most defensible framing avoids both complacency and melodrama. There is no single global tipping point beyond which the climate abruptly runs away; the palaeoclimate record contains no such episode in conditions resembling ours, and the runaway greenhouse is unreachable by fossil fuel burning. There are, however, multiple regional systems with credible threshold behaviour, largely irreversible on human timescales, whose likelihood rises with every increment of warming and whose thresholds are not known precisely enough to be steered around. The rational response to a poorly located cliff edge in fog is not to approach it slowly and carefully but to stay well back, which is the substantive argument behind a temperature target rather than a cost-benefit optimum. A related idea from dynamical systems is critical slowing down. As a system approaches a bifurcation, the restoring force weakens, so it recovers more sluggishly from small perturbations and its fluctuations grow larger and more strongly autocorrelated. In principle this offers an early-warning signal that can be measured in a time series before the transition arrives, and it has been claimed for AMOC proxies, Greenland melt and Amazon greenness. In practice the method demands long, homogeneous, low-noise records, which climate observations rarely provide, and the same statistical signature can be produced by changes in the forcing or in the observing system. The technique is promising and worth pursuing; individual published warnings based on it should be read as hypotheses rather than forecasts.

sections.heading: How Feedbacks Are Measured
sections.body: Three independent lines of evidence constrain the strength of climate feedbacks, and the modern assessment rests on their agreement rather than on any one of them. The first is process understanding, combining radiative transfer theory with direct observation. Satellite instruments such as CERES have measured the top-of-atmosphere energy budget continuously since 2000 with a precision sufficient to detect changes of a few tenths of a watt per square metre. Combining these with observed surface temperature variations allows individual feedbacks to be estimated by radiative kernel methods, which compute how much outgoing radiation changes for a unit change in temperature, humidity, cloud or albedo at each level. Argo floats, nearly four thousand of them profiling the upper 2,000 metres of the ocean since the mid-2000s, independently measure the accumulating heat and therefore the planetary energy imbalance, currently around 1 watt per square metre. The second is the historical record. Since 1850 the world has warmed about 1.3 degrees while forcings have grown, and the ratio constrains the net feedback. This approach is hampered by aerosol forcing, which is large, cooling, and the single most uncertain term in the whole forcing budget, and by the pattern effect discussed above, which makes historical feedbacks look more negative than equilibrium ones. Estimates from this route alone once suggested sensitivity near 2 degrees; correcting for both issues brings them into line with the other lines of evidence. The third is palaeoclimate. The Last Glacial Maximum around 20,000 years ago was some 5 to 7 degrees colder globally with carbon dioxide near 180 parts per million, a combination that only makes sense with substantial amplifying feedbacks. Warm periods provide the complementary test: the mid-Pliocene, about 3 million years ago, had carbon dioxide near today's 420 parts per million and was 2.5 to 4 degrees warmer with sea level perhaps 10 to 20 metres higher. The Palaeocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum 56 million years ago saw 5 to 8 degrees of warming following a carbon release of thousands of billions of tonnes over several thousand years, and is the closest geological analogue, though our release is roughly ten times faster. Global climate models tie these together but are not an independent fourth line, since they are built from the same physics and evaluated against the same observations. The 2021 assessment deliberately reduced its reliance on the raw model spread after several models in the CMIP6 generation produced sensitivities above 5 degrees that could not be reconciled with the palaeoclimate and historical constraints; those models are now generally regarded as having overly strong cloud feedbacks. A fourth technique, emergent constraints, sits between these lines. It looks for a quantity that models disagree about, that correlates across models with their sensitivity, and that can be measured in the real world — the seasonal cycle of subtropical humidity, say. Observing it then narrows the plausible range. The approach is elegant, but vulnerable to spurious correlation across a small ensemble of models sharing code and assumptions, so weight is given only where a physical mechanism links the predictor to the feedback.

sections.heading: Limits of the Framework and What It Means in Practice
sections.body: The feedback framework is a powerful simplification, and its limits should be stated plainly. It linearises a nonlinear system, assumes feedbacks add independently when several are physically coupled, reduces a spatially structured planet to a single global mean temperature, and treats as a constant a quantity that actually drifts over centuries. Each approximation is defensible for the range of warming we are likely to encounter, and each degrades as the forcing grows. A single value of climate sensitivity is a summary statistic of a particular experiment, not a physical constant of the Earth. Several practical conclusions follow robustly. Because amplifying feedbacks roughly triple the direct effect of carbon dioxide, arguments dismissing the direct forcing as small are irrelevant; it was never the issue. Because sensitivity depends inversely on the net feedback, uncertainty is not symmetric and cannot be used to argue for complacency: the same evidence that leaves open a 2.5-degree outcome leaves open a 4.5-degree one, and the damage function is convex, so the expected harm is dominated by the bad tail. Because slow feedbacks continue after fast ones have equilibrated, the warming implied by a given concentration is larger over centuries than over decades, and sea level keeps rising for many hundreds of years after temperature stabilises. Because several feedbacks are irreversible on human timescales, overshooting a temperature target and returning is not equivalent to never exceeding it. Where the science is genuinely unsettled, it is worth being specific rather than gesturing at uncertainty in general. The magnitude of the cloud feedback, the fate of subtropical stratocumulus, the threshold of the permafrost response, the stability of the West Antarctic ice sheet, the reality of marine ice cliff instability, the future of the Amazon, and the timing of any AMOC transition are live questions on which competent researchers disagree. The sign of the net feedback, the size of the water vapour and albedo terms, and the fact that amplifying feedbacks fall short of runaway are not. For anyone trying to reason about this without a laboratory, the useful discipline is to ask of any claim: is this a forcing or a feedback, on what timescale does it operate, how large is it in watts per square metre per degree compared with the 3.2 of the Planck response, and is it reversible? Claims that survive those four questions are worth taking seriously. Most of the confident assertions made in public argument, in both directions, do not survive the first one. One last stabilising feedback deserves mention for perspective. Silicate rock weathering consumes carbon dioxide, accelerating in warmer, wetter conditions and eventually locking carbon into marine carbonate. This thermostat, described by James Walker, Paul Hays and James Kasting in 1981, is why Earth has stayed habitable for billions of years despite a sun that has brightened by roughly 30 per cent. It is real, genuinely negative, and irrelevant on any timescale a person can plan around, because it works over hundreds of thousands of years. That is the shape of the whole subject: the loops that rescue us are slow, and the loops that amplify us are fast.

guides.title: Global Warming — Causes and Evidence
guides.summary: An explanation of the physical mechanism that warms the planet and the observational evidence that establishes it, covering the greenhouse effect, the carbon cycle, the human fingerprint in the atmosphere, the temperature and paleoclimate records, feedbacks, climate models, and the alternative explanations that have been tested and found wanting.

sections.heading: What Global Warming Is, and What It Is Not
sections.body: Global warming is the sustained increase in the average temperature of the Earth's lower atmosphere and oceans caused by a change in the planet's energy balance. Since the late nineteenth century the global mean surface temperature has risen by roughly 1.2 to 1.3 degrees Celsius, with most of that increase occurring after 1975. The number sounds small, and the smallness of it is the first thing a reader needs to have explained, because it is the most common reason the subject is dismissed. A global average is not a local forecast. The difference between a mild winter day and a cold one might be fifteen degrees, but that is one place at one moment. A global annual average pools the entire planet across an entire year, and it is extremely stable; during the depths of the last ice age, when a kilometre of ice sat over Chicago and sea level was 120 metres lower, the global average was only about 5 to 6 degrees below the pre-industrial value. A single degree of global average change is therefore roughly a fifth of the difference between the present world and an ice age, delivered in about a century rather than over five thousand years. Rate matters as much as magnitude. It is also essential to separate weather from climate. Weather is the state of the atmosphere over hours to weeks and is chaotic in the technical sense, meaning that tiny differences in initial conditions amplify until prediction fails after roughly ten days. Climate is the statistical distribution of weather over decades, and it is governed by boundary conditions such as how much energy arrives from the Sun and how readily the atmosphere lets heat escape. The standard analogy is that you cannot predict whether a particular person will die next Tuesday but actuaries predict mortality rates for millions with precision. A cold week in April tells you nothing about the trend, and warming does not abolish winter. The reason this matters practically is that the consequences do not arrive as a uniform gentle warming. They arrive as shifts in the distribution: heat extremes that were once rare becoming common, heavier rainfall when it does rain because a warmer atmosphere holds about seven per cent more water vapour per degree, longer droughts in already dry subtropical belts, rising seas, and acidifying oceans. Warming is not evenly distributed either. Land warms faster than ocean because water has enormous heat capacity and evaporates, and the Arctic has warmed roughly three to four times the global rate, a phenomenon called Arctic amplification. Understanding the subject properly means understanding the mechanism, not memorising the conclusion, and the mechanism is nineteenth-century physics that can be demonstrated in a laboratory.

sections.heading: The Greenhouse Effect: The Physics of an Energy Balance
sections.body: The Earth's temperature is set by a simple accounting problem: energy in must equal energy out, or the planet heats or cools until it does. Energy arrives almost entirely as sunlight. At the top of the atmosphere the incoming flux, the solar constant, averages about 1,361 watts per square metre facing the Sun. Because a sphere has four times the surface area of the disc it presents, the average over the whole globe is about 340 watts per square metre. Roughly thirty per cent of that is reflected straight back to space by clouds, ice, deserts and the atmosphere itself, a fraction called the albedo, leaving about 240 watts per square metre absorbed. Everything with a temperature radiates. The Stefan-Boltzmann law states that the power radiated per unit area equals a constant, 5.67 times ten to the minus eight, multiplied by the absolute temperature raised to the fourth power. Setting outgoing radiation equal to the 240 watts absorbed gives an effective radiating temperature of about 255 kelvin, or minus 18 degrees Celsius. That is what the Earth would be without an atmosphere, and it is well below freezing everywhere. The actual global mean surface temperature is about 15 degrees Celsius. The 33-degree gap is the natural greenhouse effect, and without it the planet would be a frozen ball. The mechanism is a difference in wavelength. Sunlight is emitted by a surface at roughly 5,800 kelvin and so peaks in the visible, around 500 nanometres, which passes through the atmosphere largely unimpeded. The Earth, at around 288 kelvin, radiates in the thermal infrared, peaking near 10 micrometres. Certain gases are nearly transparent to incoming visible light but strongly absorb outgoing infrared. They absorb that radiation and re-emit it in all directions, including downward, so the surface receives energy from both the Sun and the atmosphere. The most precise way to state the effect avoids the misleading blanket metaphor. Adding greenhouse gas raises the altitude at which the atmosphere becomes transparent enough for infrared radiation to escape to space. Because temperature falls with height in the troposphere at roughly 6.5 degrees per kilometre, that higher emission level is colder, and a colder emitter radiates less. The planet is then absorbing more than it emits, and it must warm throughout the lower atmosphere until the emission level is back at the temperature needed to radiate 240 watts per square metre. Doubling carbon dioxide reduces outgoing radiation by about 3.7 watts per square metre, a figure calculated from line-by-line radiative transfer using measured absorption spectra and confirmed by satellite and surface observations. None of this is speculative chemistry. The absorption bands of carbon dioxide were measured in the laboratory in the nineteenth century, are used every day in engineering, and are the reason infrared gas analysers and heat-seeking optics have to be designed around them.

sections.heading: Which Gases Matter, and Why Molecules Absorb Infrared
sections.body: Not every gas is a greenhouse gas, and the reason is molecular structure. For a molecule to absorb infrared radiation it must have a vibrational mode that changes its electric dipole moment, so that the oscillating electric field of the light can push on it. Nitrogen and oxygen, which together make up about 99 per cent of the atmosphere, are symmetric two-atom molecules with no dipole moment and no way to acquire one by stretching, so they are essentially transparent to infrared. This is why the bulk of the air plays no direct radiative role. Molecules with three or more atoms, such as water vapour, carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide and ozone, have bending and asymmetric stretching modes that do create a transient dipole, and they absorb strongly. Carbon dioxide's bending mode absorbs near 15 micrometres, close to the peak of Earth's outgoing radiation, which is what makes a trace gas so consequential. Water vapour is the largest contributor to the natural greenhouse effect, supplying roughly half, with clouds adding perhaps a quarter and carbon dioxide about a fifth. This fact is often deployed as though it were an objection, and understanding why it is not is central. Water vapour has a residence time in the atmosphere of about nine days, and the amount the air can hold is set by temperature through the Clausius-Clapeyron relation, roughly seven per cent more per degree of warming. Add water vapour and it rains out within a fortnight; the concentration is a consequence of temperature, not an independent control on it. Water vapour is therefore a powerful feedback that roughly doubles any initial warming, but it cannot initiate a change. Carbon dioxide, which does not condense at terrestrial temperatures and whose excess persists for centuries to millennia, is the control knob. The concentrations are worth stating precisely. Carbon dioxide stood near 280 parts per million through the Holocene before industrialisation and passed 420 parts per million in the 2020s, an increase of about fifty per cent. Methane has risen from about 720 parts per billion to over 1,900, more than doubling. Nitrous oxide has gone from roughly 270 to about 335 parts per billion. Gases are compared using global warming potential, the heat trapped by a mass of gas relative to the same mass of carbon dioxide over a chosen horizon, usually a hundred years. On that basis methane is about 28 times as potent, nitrous oxide about 273, and industrial fluorinated gases such as sulphur hexafluoride many thousands. Methane's short lifetime of roughly twelve years means cutting it produces relatively fast relief, whereas carbon dioxide commitments are effectively permanent on human timescales.

sections.heading: The Carbon Cycle and Where the Extra Carbon Goes
sections.body: Carbon moves constantly between the atmosphere, the oceans, land vegetation and soils, and rocks. The natural fluxes are large. Photosynthesis draws roughly 120 billion tonnes of carbon out of the air each year and respiration and decay return nearly the same; the ocean surface exchanges roughly 80 billion tonnes each way. Because these flows are large and nearly balanced, a common objection holds that human emissions of about 10 to 11 billion tonnes of carbon per year are trivial by comparison. The error is confusing a flux with a net imbalance. A household with income and spending of fifty thousand a year is not unaffected by an extra thousand of debt annually; it accumulates. Natural exchanges cancel; human emissions do not. The accumulation is directly observed. Of each year's human emissions, roughly a quarter is absorbed by the oceans and roughly a further quarter to a third by land vegetation, leaving about forty-five per cent in the air. That fraction is called the airborne fraction and it has stayed broadly stable for decades, though there are signs some sinks are weakening. The ocean uptake happens because carbon dioxide dissolves and reacts with water to form carbonic acid, which dissociates; this is also why ocean pH has fallen from about 8.2 to about 8.1 since pre-industrial times, a thirty per cent increase in hydrogen ion concentration, because the pH scale is logarithmic. Ocean acidification is the second, less discussed consequence of the same emissions, and it is a direct chemical measurement, not a model output. The timescale for removal is the crucial and widely misunderstood part. Individual carbon dioxide molecules cycle in and out of the ocean within a few years, and this rapid exchange is sometimes quoted as the lifetime. What matters is how long a pulse of added carbon perturbs the total. Roughly half of an emitted pulse is drawn down within a few decades, a further portion over centuries as the deep ocean overturns, and the remaining fifteen to thirty per cent persists for many thousands of years until slow silicate rock weathering removes it. Practically speaking, a substantial fraction of the carbon dioxide released by burning coal today will still be affecting the climate when the descendants of everyone now alive are as remote from us as we are from the Bronze Age. The sources are well quantified. Fossil fuel combustion and cement production dominate, with land-use change, chiefly deforestation, contributing roughly a tenth of current emissions. Cement is a distinctive case because calcining limestone releases carbon dioxide from the rock itself, independent of the fuel used to heat the kiln, and accounts for something like seven or eight per cent of the global total.

sections.heading: The Human Fingerprint: How We Know the Carbon Is Ours
sections.body: That carbon dioxide is rising is a measurement; that the rise is caused by human activity is an inference, but a strongly overdetermined one, resting on several independent lines of evidence that would all have to be wrong together. The first is simple accounting. The quantity of fossil carbon extracted and burned is tracked by industry and tax authorities and is roughly twice the observed atmospheric increase. The problem is not explaining where the extra carbon came from but explaining where half of it went, which the ocean and land sinks do. The second is isotopic. Carbon has three isotopes: stable carbon-12 and carbon-13, and radioactive carbon-14 with a half-life of 5,730 years. Photosynthesis discriminates slightly against the heavier carbon-13, so plant material, and therefore the fossil fuels made from ancient plant material, is depleted in carbon-13. As fossil carbon enters the air, the ratio of carbon-13 to carbon-12 in the atmosphere should fall, and it does, measurably and continuously; this is called the Suess effect. Meanwhile fossil fuels are hundreds of millions of years old, so all their carbon-14 has decayed away. Adding that dead carbon dilutes atmospheric carbon-14, and tree rings record exactly that decline through the industrial era, before atomic-weapons testing complicated the signal after 1950. Volcanic carbon has a different isotopic signature, and volcanoes in any case emit on the order of 0.3 to 0.4 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide annually, roughly one per cent of human emissions. The third is oxygen. Burning carbon consumes oxygen in a fixed stoichiometric ratio. Precise atmospheric oxygen measurements, pioneered by Ralph Keeling from the late 1980s, show a decline of a few parts per million per year, in the amount predicted by fuel combustion. If the carbon dioxide rise came from oceanic outgassing rather than combustion, atmospheric oxygen would not fall at all. The fourth is the pattern of warming itself, which distinguishes a greenhouse cause from a solar one. If the Sun were brightening, the entire atmosphere would warm. Instead the troposphere warms while the stratosphere above it cools, by roughly half a degree per decade in the upper stratosphere, exactly as greenhouse theory requires because the higher layers are radiating more efficiently to space while being cut off from surface heat. Nights warm faster than days, winters faster than summers, and the Arctic faster than the tropics. Satellites measure less infrared escaping to space precisely in the carbon dioxide absorption bands, and surface instruments measure more infrared coming down in those same bands. That is the mechanism caught in the act. Taken together these fingerprints are not four restatements of one argument but four independent measurements from different instruments and different scientific disciplines, and any alternative explanation would have to account for all of them simultaneously while also explaining why the well-established radiative physics of carbon dioxide somehow fails to operate.

sections.heading: A Two-Century Scientific History
sections.body: Climate science is not a recent political creation; its foundations are older than the theory of evolution by natural selection and older than the germ theory of disease. Joseph Fourier, the French mathematician, asked in the 1820s why the Earth is warmer than a bare calculation of solar heating suggests, and proposed that the atmosphere traps heat much as glass in a hothouse does. His analogy was physically inexact, since a greenhouse works mainly by preventing convection, but the question and the conclusion were right. Eunice Newton Foote, an American scientist, published in 1856 the results of a simple experiment: glass cylinders filled with different gases and placed in sunlight warmed differently, and the one containing carbon dioxide became hottest and held its heat longest. She wrote that an atmosphere of that gas would give the Earth a high temperature. Her paper was read for her at a scientific meeting because women were not permitted to present, and was long forgotten. John Tyndall, working in London, built a far more precise apparatus, a ratio spectrophotometer, and demonstrated in 1859 that nitrogen and oxygen are transparent to radiant heat while water vapour, carbon dioxide and hydrocarbons absorb it strongly. This is the laboratory foundation of the whole subject. Svante Arrhenius, a Swedish chemist, performed in 1896 the first quantitative calculation of how much the surface would warm if carbon dioxide doubled, working through thousands of hand computations. He obtained about 5 to 6 degrees Celsius, high compared with modern estimates but the right order of magnitude, and he recognised the water vapour feedback and the ice-albedo feedback. He expected the change would take millennia and thought a warmer Sweden might be pleasant. Guy Callendar, a British steam engineer, compiled temperature records in 1938 and argued that warming was already detectable and attributable to fuel burning; he was politely doubted. The modern era began with measurement. Charles David Keeling started continuous carbon dioxide monitoring at Mauna Loa in Hawaii in 1958, producing the sawtooth Keeling curve whose annual wiggle is the northern hemisphere's forests breathing in and out and whose relentless upward trend settled the question of accumulation. In 1979 the United States National Academy of Sciences convened the Charney panel, which concluded that doubling carbon dioxide would warm the planet by 1.5 to 4.5 degrees. That range barely moved for forty years, which is either an indictment of progress or a striking demonstration of robustness. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change was established in 1988 to assess the literature; it conducts no research of its own but synthesises thousands of published papers, and its reports are approved line by line by member governments, a process that tends to produce conservative rather than alarmist wording. The point worth holding onto is that every essential element of the theory, the absorption physics, the calculation of sensitivity, and the prediction that fossil fuel burning would warm the planet, was in place long before any of it became politically contentious.

sections.heading: Building the Temperature Record and Testing It for Bias
sections.body: The global temperature record is assembled from tens of thousands of land weather stations, ships, drifting and moored buoys, and Argo floats, some of which have been reporting since the 1850s. Turning that heterogeneous pile into a single trustworthy curve requires care, and the objections raised against it are reasonable ones that scientists themselves raised first. The central technique is anomaly averaging. Rather than averaging absolute temperatures, which vary hugely between a mountain station and a coastal one, each station's departure from its own long-term baseline is computed and those departures are averaged. Anomalies are spatially coherent over hundreds of kilometres, so a sparse network still captures the large-scale signal, and a station's altitude or local microclimate cancels out. Records are then homogenised to remove artificial jumps caused by a station moving, a thermometer being replaced, or the observation time changing; such breaks are detected statistically by comparison with neighbouring stations. Adjustments are published and their code is open. Notably, the net effect of all adjustments on the global ocean record is to reduce the apparent warming trend, not increase it, because early ship measurements taken by hauling up canvas buckets read artificially cool through evaporation and had to be corrected upward, making the past warmer. The urban heat island effect is real: cities are genuinely warmer than surrounding countryside by up to several degrees because of dark surfaces, reduced evaporation and waste heat. The question is whether it contaminates the trend. It is tested by comparing rural-only station subsets with the full network, by comparing windy nights with calm nights, and by checking against ocean data where no cities exist. The trends agree. In 2010 a group led by physicist Richard Muller, funded partly by donors sceptical of the consensus, reanalysed the raw data independently as the Berkeley Earth project specifically to test these objections, and reproduced the existing results closely. Muller publicly changed his position. Independence matters. At least six groups, including NASA GISS, NOAA, the UK Met Office and Climatic Research Unit, Berkeley Earth, the Japan Meteorological Agency and the European Copernicus service, produce records using different station selections and different methods, and they agree within a few hundredths of a degree. Satellite microwave sounding units, which infer bulk atmospheric temperature from oxygen emission rather than measuring the surface at all, independently show warming; an early discrepancy in that record was traced in 2005 to an uncorrected sign error in the orbital decay adjustment. Reanalysis products, borehole temperature profiles, sea level rise, and the retreat of glaciers on every continent all corroborate the same trend through entirely different physics. There are also biological witnesses that keep no instruments at all: the dates of cherry blossom in Kyoto, recorded in court diaries since the ninth century, the earlier arrival of migratory birds, the poleward and upslope shift of species ranges, and the lengthening growing season all register the same change.

sections.heading: Deep Time: What Ice Cores and Other Archives Show
sections.body: Instrumental records cover under two centuries. To know whether the current change is unusual, and to see how the climate system has behaved under different conditions, scientists read natural archives that record past climate, a field called paleoclimatology. The best of these are ice cores. Snow falling on the Antarctic and Greenland ice sheets compacts into ice, trapping bubbles of the actual ancient atmosphere. Drilling recovers a continuous column: the EPICA Dome C core in Antarctica reaches back about 800,000 years, and recent blue-ice and deep-drilling work extends fragments beyond a million. Counting annual layers, visible as seasonal changes in dust and isotopes, gives dating comparable to tree rings for recent millennia. Extracting the trapped air and analysing it gives a direct measurement, not a proxy, of past carbon dioxide and methane. The result is unambiguous: through eight glacial cycles carbon dioxide oscillated between roughly 180 parts per million in glacial maxima and 280 to 300 in warm interglacials, and never once exceeded about 300. The present 420-plus is far outside that entire range, and the rate of increase is roughly a hundred times faster than the fastest natural transitions in the record. Temperature comes from isotopes in the ice itself. Water containing the heavier oxygen-18 or deuterium condenses preferentially, so colder conditions leave snow more depleted in heavy isotopes; the relationship is calibrated against modern observations. The cores also show that during the ice ages the primary trigger was not carbon dioxide but orbital variation, the Milankovitch cycles: changes in the shape of Earth's orbit over about 100,000 years, the tilt of its axis between 22.1 and 24.5 degrees over 41,000 years, and the precession of the axis over roughly 23,000 years. These redistribute sunlight by season and latitude without much changing the total. The modest orbital nudge is then amplified by feedbacks, chiefly ice albedo and the ocean's release or uptake of carbon dioxide, which is why carbon dioxide lags temperature by several centuries at the start of a deglaciation while still supplying most of the eventual warming. That lag is often quoted as though it refutes the greenhouse effect; it does the opposite, demonstrating that carbon dioxide is a powerful amplifier. Orbital forcing today is slightly negative, so it cannot explain current warming. Other archives cross-check the picture. Tree rings, corals, cave formations, lake and ocean sediments, pollen assemblages and borehole temperature profiles each have different strengths and weaknesses, and reconstructions combining them show the last few decades to be warmer than any comparable period in at least the last two thousand years, and probably considerably longer. Going further back, the geological record offers a sobering analogue in the Paleocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum of about 56 million years ago, when a large release of carbon warmed the planet by roughly 5 degrees, acidified the oceans and triggered deep-sea extinctions. Even that event released carbon at perhaps a tenth of the current rate.

sections.heading: Radiative Forcing and Climate Sensitivity
sections.body: To compare causes of climate change on a common footing, scientists use radiative forcing, measured in watts per square metre: the change in the planet's net energy balance at the top of the atmosphere caused by some factor, before the climate responds. Positive forcing warms, negative cools. Doubling carbon dioxide gives about 3.7 watts per square metre. Total human forcing since 1750 is approximately 2.7 watts per square metre, of which greenhouse gases contribute more, partly offset by roughly minus 1 watt per square metre from aerosols, the sulphate and soot particles emitted alongside, which reflect sunlight and seed brighter clouds. Change in solar output over the same period contributes on the order of 0.05 watts per square metre, perhaps two per cent of the human total. Climate sensitivity is the response to that forcing, and it is the single most consequential number in the field. Equilibrium climate sensitivity, ECS, is the eventual warming after a doubling of carbon dioxide once the system has fully adjusted, which takes centuries because the deep ocean is slow to heat. Transient climate response, TCR, is the warming at the moment of doubling under a steady one per cent annual increase, and is more relevant to this century; it is typically about 1.4 to 2.2 degrees. The IPCC's Sixth Assessment Report in 2021 narrowed ECS to a likely range of 2.5 to 4 degrees Celsius, with a best estimate of 3, tightening the long-standing 1.5 to 4.5 band for the first time in four decades. The arithmetic of why sensitivity exceeds the bare radiative effect is worth following. A forcing of 3.7 watts per square metre, acting on the Stefan-Boltzmann response of a 288-kelvin planet, would by itself raise temperature by roughly 1.1 degrees. Everything above that comes from feedbacks. The estimate is constrained by three largely independent approaches: process understanding and models; the historical record of warming since 1850 combined with known forcings; and paleoclimate evidence from the Last Glacial Maximum and from much warmer past epochs.
