These agree well enough to exclude both very low and very high values, though the upper tail is harder to rule out than the lower. The residual uncertainty is not comforting. A low sensitivity would buy time; a high one would be catastrophic; and the distribution is skewed such that the bad tail is longer than the good one. Policy has to be made against that asymmetry, which is fundamentally a risk management problem rather than a prediction problem. Aerosols are the largest single source of uncertainty in the historical constraint, because their cooling effect is poorly quantified, particularly the indirect effect on cloud brightness. This has an uncomfortable implication: air pollution has been masking part of the warming already committed, so cleaning up sulphate emissions, which is unambiguously good for human lungs, unmasks additional warming. A reduction in shipping fuel sulphur content in 2020 appears to have produced a small, detectable step of this kind over the shipping lanes of the North Atlantic and Pacific.

sections.heading: Feedbacks: What Amplifies and What Restrains the Warming
sections.body: A feedback is a process triggered by warming that then affects warming further. Positive feedbacks amplify, negative ones damp. The overall sensitivity of the climate is essentially a question of which dominate and by how much, and this is where most of the genuine scientific difficulty lies. The single most important negative feedback is the Planck response, the fact that a warmer surface radiates more energy in proportion to the fourth power of absolute temperature. This is what makes the climate stable rather than runaway, and it is worth stating clearly because the fear of a Venus-like runaway on Earth is not supported; Earth is too far from the Sun and its oceans could not be boiled off by any plausible emission of carbon. The largest positive feedback is water vapour. Warming raises the saturation vapour pressure by roughly seven per cent per degree, relative humidity stays approximately constant, and the extra vapour, being a potent greenhouse gas, adds further forcing. Alone this roughly doubles the direct effect of carbon dioxide. It is partly offset by the lapse rate feedback: in the tropics the upper troposphere warms faster than the surface, raising the effective radiating temperature and letting more heat escape. The two are physically linked and are usually assessed together, giving a combined positive contribution. Ice albedo is the most intuitive. Fresh snow reflects perhaps eighty to ninety per cent of incoming sunlight; open ocean reflects about six per cent and absorbs the rest. Melting ice therefore exposes a dark surface that absorbs more energy and drives further melting. Arctic sea ice extent at the September minimum has declined by roughly forty per cent since satellite records began in 1979, and volume has fallen considerably more. This feedback is the main reason the Arctic warms several times faster than the global mean. Clouds are the hardest problem in the field and the dominant source of spread between climate models. Clouds both reflect sunlight, cooling, and trap infrared, warming. Which effect wins depends on altitude, thickness and droplet size: low thick marine stratocumulus cool strongly, high thin cirrus warm. Whether warming produces more or fewer of each is not fully resolved, though the weight of recent evidence, from satellite observations and from high-resolution simulations that resolve individual clouds, suggests the net cloud feedback is positive, which is part of why the sensitivity estimate was nudged upward. Finally there are carbon cycle feedbacks, which matter over longer horizons. Permafrost across Siberia, Alaska and Canada holds an estimated 1,400 to 1,600 billion tonnes of carbon, roughly twice what is currently in the atmosphere; thawing releases some as carbon dioxide and some, in waterlogged conditions, as methane. Warmer oceans dissolve less gas, and stressed forests take up less. These are considered likely to be gradual rather than explosive, but they add to the committed warming.

sections.heading: Observed Consequences Beyond the Thermometer
sections.body: Surface temperature is only one indicator, and by itself a noisy one because the atmosphere holds very little heat. Roughly ninety per cent of the extra energy trapped by the enhanced greenhouse effect has gone into the ocean, and ocean heat content is the cleanest single measure of the planetary energy imbalance. Since 2000 the Argo array of nearly four thousand autonomous floats has profiled the upper two thousand metres every ten days worldwide, and it shows a steady, monotonic rise with far less year-to-year noise than the surface record. This is why the so-called warming pause of the early 2000s was never a pause in the energy balance; heat was going into the deeper ocean, and surface temperatures resumed climbing sharply afterwards. Sea level is rising for two distinct reasons that must be counted separately. The first is thermal expansion: water expands as it warms, and since the ocean averages nearly 3,700 metres deep, even slight warming raises the surface. The second is added mass from melting land ice. Global mean sea level rose about 1.4 millimetres per year through most of the twentieth century and is now rising at roughly 4.5 millimetres per year, measured since 1993 by satellite altimeters that bounce radar off the surface with centimetre precision, cross-checked by tide gauges. That acceleration is itself the significant finding. Greenland is losing roughly 270 billion tonnes of ice per year and Antarctica about 150 billion, measured independently by the GRACE satellite pair, which detects the minute gravitational tug of the ice, by altimetry, and by mass budget accounting. Glaciers are retreating on every continent that has them, a change documented photographically over more than a century and of practical consequence for the roughly two billion people whose dry-season water comes from mountain snow and ice. Ocean chemistry is shifting as described by carbonate equilibrium, making it harder for corals, pteropods and shellfish to build calcium carbonate structures. Marine heatwaves have driven repeated mass coral bleaching on the Great Barrier Reef, in 1998, 2002, 2016, 2017, 2020 and again since. Atmospheric circulation is shifting too: the Hadley cells are widening, pushing subtropical dry zones poleward; the growing season in the northern mid-latitudes has lengthened by roughly two weeks; and the heaviest rainfall events are intensifying because a warmer atmosphere holds more moisture, so when conditions do produce rain there is more available to fall. The pattern of drier dry areas and wetter wet ones is one of the most robust projections and is already visible in observations. Tropical cyclones are a subtler case worth stating carefully: the evidence does not show a clear increase in how many form, but it does indicate that a larger fraction reach the highest intensities, that they intensify more rapidly, that they carry more rainfall, and that their storm surges ride on a higher baseline sea level.

sections.heading: Attribution: Assigning Causes to Trends and to Single Events
sections.body: Attribution is the formal science of asking what caused an observed change, and it comes in two rather different varieties which are often confused. The first is attribution of the long-term trend, done by fingerprinting. Each possible cause leaves a distinctive spatial and vertical pattern. Increased solar output warms the whole atmospheric column including the stratosphere; greenhouse gases warm the troposphere while cooling the stratosphere. Volcanic eruptions produce short sharp cooling with a characteristic recovery. Internal ocean variability shifts heat between reservoirs but does not create it. By comparing the observed multi-dimensional pattern against these template fingerprints using regression techniques, and by running models with and without human forcings, scientists can determine which combination is consistent with the record. Simulations that include only natural factors track observations well until about 1960 and then diverge sharply, remaining flat while reality climbs. Only runs including human forcings reproduce the observed curve. The IPCC's conclusion that it is extremely likely that human influence is the dominant cause of observed warming since the mid-twentieth century, later strengthened to unequivocal, rests on this analysis. Best estimates place the human contribution at essentially all of the observed warming, since natural factors alone would have produced slight cooling. The second variety is extreme event attribution, a field that barely existed before 2004 and is now routine. It does not claim that climate change caused a particular flood, which is not a well-formed question, since weather has many contributing causes. Instead it asks how the probability or intensity of such an event has changed. The method runs large ensembles of simulations of the world as it is and of a counterfactual world without human emissions, and compares how often the event occurs in each. The result is expressed as a fraction of attributable risk or a change in return period. The Pacific Northwest heat dome of June 2021, which reached 49.6 degrees Celsius at Lytton in British Columbia, was assessed as virtually impossible without human influence. The European heatwave of 2003 was roughly twice as likely. The technique's limits should be stated honestly. Attribution is strongest for heat, where the physics is direct, moderately strong for heavy rainfall and drought, and weakest for tornadoes and for the frequency, as opposed to the intensity, of tropical cyclones, where observational records are short and mechanisms are complex. A responsible attribution study reports these confidence levels explicitly, and a well-conducted one will sometimes conclude that no human influence is detectable in a given event, which is exactly what gives the positive findings their credibility. Attribution studies have also begun to be used in litigation and in loss-and-damage negotiations, which places an unusually heavy burden on their methodology and has driven the field toward pre-registered protocols and rapid, transparent publication.

sections.heading: How Climate Models Work and How They Are Tested
sections.body: A general circulation model divides the atmosphere and ocean into a three-dimensional grid, typically with horizontal cells of 25 to 100 kilometres and several dozen vertical levels, and steps forward in time solving the fundamental equations of fluid motion, thermodynamics and radiative transfer in each cell. These are not statistical extrapolations of past temperature; they are physics simulations built from the Navier-Stokes equations, conservation of mass and energy, and laboratory-measured absorption spectra. A century-long run at high resolution consumes millions of processor-hours. Processes smaller than a grid cell cannot be resolved and must be parameterised, meaning represented by simplified relationships tuned to observations. Individual clouds, convective thunderstorms, turbulence and aerosol microphysics all fall into this category, and parameterisation is the main source of divergence between models. This is a genuine limitation and is stated as such in the literature. The standard response is the ensemble: dozens of independently developed models from different countries, with different code and different parameterisation choices, are run on identical scenarios in the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project. Where they agree, confidence is high; where they disagree, the spread is reported as the uncertainty. Models are tested in several demanding ways. They must reproduce the current climate's basic features without being told them: the jet streams, monsoons, the seasonal cycle, El Nino, the general pattern of deserts and rainforests. They must reproduce past climates, including the Last Glacial Maximum and the mid-Holocene, when boundary conditions differed greatly. And they must reproduce specific unplanned natural experiments. The eruption of Mount Pinatubo in June 1991 injected about 20 million tonnes of sulphur dioxide into the stratosphere; James Hansen's team used a model to predict a global cooling of roughly 0.5 degrees followed by recovery over two to three years, published before it happened, and observations matched closely. The strongest test is the record of old predictions. Hansen's 1988 congressional testimony presented three scenarios; the emissions path actually followed lay near his scenario B, and the warming it projected has proved close to observation once the scenario mismatch is accounted for. A 2019 study by Zeke Hausfather and colleagues evaluated seventeen projections published between 1970 and 2007 and found that most were consistent with subsequent observations, with fourteen of them statistically indistinguishable once actual emissions were substituted for assumed ones. Models also correctly predicted in advance stratospheric cooling, Arctic amplification, greater warming of nights than days, and the poleward expansion of the subtropics, each of which was subsequently observed. Successful prediction of phenomena not used in construction is the strongest evidence available that a model captures real physics. It is also worth noting that the broad conclusion does not depend on these large models at all. Simple energy-balance calculations of the kind Arrhenius performed by hand, and observational estimates from the historical record and from paleoclimate, arrive at similar sensitivities. The models add regional detail, seasonal structure and process understanding; they are not the foundation of the case.

sections.heading: Alternative Explanations That Have Been Tested and Rejected
sections.body: Good science requires taking rival explanations seriously and testing them, and every proposed natural cause of the current warming has been examined. Each fails on measurement, not on assertion. The Sun is the obvious candidate and the most thoroughly checked. Total solar irradiance has been measured directly by satellites since 1978 with sufficient precision to track the eleven-year sunspot cycle, whose amplitude is about 0.1 per cent, roughly 0.2 watts per square metre in forcing. Solar activity rose during the first half of the twentieth century and contributed to early warming, then plateaued and slightly declined from about 1980, while temperature climbed steeply. The two have moved in opposite directions for four decades. The pattern test is decisive as well: a brighter Sun warms the stratosphere, whereas the stratosphere has cooled. The cosmic ray hypothesis, developed by Henrik Svensmark, proposes that galactic cosmic rays seed cloud nuclei and that a stronger solar magnetic field, by deflecting them, reduces cloudiness and warms the planet. It is a physically coherent idea and it was tested seriously, including at the CERN CLOUD experiment, which built a chamber specifically to measure ion-induced nucleation. The result was that ions do affect nucleation rates modestly but the effect on the number of cloud condensation nuclei is far too small to explain observed warming, and in any case the cosmic ray flux shows no trend matching the temperature record. Volcanoes emit carbon dioxide, but at roughly 0.3 to 0.4 billion tonnes annually against human emissions of about 37 billion. Their net climate effect is cooling, through stratospheric sulphate aerosols, and it lasts only a few years. Ocean cycles such as the El Nino Southern Oscillation, the Pacific Decadal Oscillation and the Atlantic Multidecadal Oscillation redistribute existing heat between ocean and atmosphere, which is why a strong El Nino year is warm and a La Nina year cooler. They cannot add energy to the system, and if they were the cause, ocean heat content would fall as the surface warmed. It rises. The suggestion that the planet is simply recovering from the Little Ice Age has no mechanism attached; climate does not drift back to a preferred state without a physical cause, and the cause of the cooling, a combination of volcanic activity and a solar minimum, has not reversed. Orbital forcing is currently slightly negative, meaning that without human influence the very long-term trend would be gentle cooling toward the next glaciation. One further claim deserves direct treatment because it sounds technical: that the carbon dioxide absorption bands are already saturated, so adding more can have no effect. The central part of the fifteen-micrometre band is indeed nearly opaque at the surface, but this misunderstands where emission to space occurs. Radiation escapes from the thin upper atmosphere, not the surface, and adding gas raises that escape altitude into colder air, reducing outgoing radiation. The band also has wings that are not saturated and broaden as concentration rises, which is why the forcing grows with the logarithm of concentration rather than stopping, and why each doubling adds a similar increment of warming.

sections.heading: Scenarios, Carbon Budgets and Tipping Points
sections.body: Because future emissions depend on choices rather than physics, projections are made under scenarios. The current framework uses Shared Socioeconomic Pathways paired with forcing levels, labelled for instance SSP1-1.9 for very rapid decarbonisation reaching about 1.9 watts per square metre of forcing, up to SSP5-8.5 for a fossil-fuel-intensive world. It is important to understand that these are not predictions or probabilities but conditional statements: if emissions follow this path, the climate is expected to respond in this way. SSP5-8.5 in particular is often misreported as a business-as-usual forecast; it was designed as a deliberately high-end reference case and current policy trajectories fall well below it, though also well above the low pathways. The most useful concept for policy is the carbon budget. Because warming is close to linearly proportional to cumulative emissions, roughly 0.45 degrees per thousand billion tonnes of carbon dioxide, there is a finite total that can be emitted for any temperature limit. Staying below 1.5 degrees with even odds corresponds to a remaining budget of a few hundred billion tonnes from the mid-2020s, against annual emissions near 40 billion. That is under a decade at current rates, which is the arithmetic behind the urgency of the target. The near-linear relationship also carries a hopeful implication: warming stops approximately when net emissions reach zero, because the ocean and land continue absorbing carbon as the radiative imbalance closes. Warming is not locked in for centuries regardless of action, though sea level rise and ice sheet loss continue for far longer. Tipping points are thresholds beyond which a component of the system shifts to a different state that persists even if the forcing is removed. Candidates include the collapse of the West Antarctic and Greenland ice sheets, the dieback of the Amazon rainforest, widespread permafrost thaw, the loss of tropical coral reefs, and a slowdown or collapse of the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation, the current system that includes the Gulf Stream. Honesty requires several qualifications. The thresholds are poorly known, estimates range widely, several of these transitions would unfold over centuries rather than abruptly, and the popular image of a sudden global catastrophe is not what most of the literature supports. What the literature does support is that the probability of crossing such thresholds rises with temperature, that the consequences would be effectively irreversible on human timescales, and that this asymmetry is the strongest argument for limiting warming rather than adapting to whatever arrives. Two practical points follow. First, temperature targets such as 1.5 and 2 degrees are political thresholds chosen from a continuum of risk, not physical cliff edges; 1.6 degrees is not a catastrophe and 1.4 is not safety, and every tenth of a degree avoided reduces harm proportionately. Exceeding a target is therefore a reason to continue reducing emissions, not to abandon the effort. Second, the distinction between mitigation, reducing emissions, and adaptation, preparing for the warming already committed, is not a choice between alternatives. Some warming is already unavoidable, so adaptation is necessary regardless, and adaptation has limits that rise steeply with temperature, so mitigation determines how much adaptation will be possible at all.

sections.heading: Genuine Uncertainties, and How the Evidence Gets Misread
sections.body: A guide that presented this subject as entirely settled would be misleading, so it is worth separating what is essentially certain from what is not. The radiative physics of carbon dioxide, the observed rise in concentration, the human origin of that rise, and the fact of warming are as securely established as anything in the earth sciences; disputing them requires disputing laboratory spectroscopy and direct measurement. Substantially less certain are the exact value of climate sensitivity within its likely range, the magnitude of the aerosol offset, the sign and size of specific cloud feedbacks, the behaviour of ice sheets and therefore the upper bound of sea level rise this century, regional precipitation changes at the scale of individual river basins, the locations and thresholds of tipping points, and the response of tropical cyclone frequency. The characteristic ways this evidence gets misread are worth recognising because they recur. Cherry-picking short intervals is the most common: the temperature record contains substantial year-to-year variability from El Nino and volcanic eruptions, so a trend line drawn from an exceptionally warm year such as 1998 to a cooler later year can appear flat while the underlying thirty-year trend is unchanged. The remedy is to insist on periods of at least thirty years, the standard climatological averaging window, and to look at ocean heat content, which is far less noisy. A second pattern is treating a single unresolved detail as though it invalidated the whole structure; the evidence is a converging network from many disciplines, and pulling one thread does not unravel it. A third is confusing the greenhouse mechanism with a claim that carbon dioxide is the only thing affecting climate, which no scientist asserts. A fourth is the appeal to past natural climate change as evidence that the present change is natural, which is like arguing that because forests have always burned from lightning, no fire can be arson. On the other side, exaggeration also does damage. Claims that human extinction is imminent, that particular cities will certainly be underwater by a specific near date, or that any given storm was simply caused by climate change go beyond what the evidence supports and, when they fail to materialise, corrode trust in the parts that are solid. The disciplined position is to state confidence levels explicitly, distinguish observation from projection, distinguish projection from scenario, and be willing to say plainly that a particular question is not yet answered. For a reader wanting to evaluate a claim independently, a few habits help more than any amount of argument. Ask what is being measured and by what instrument. Ask over what period a trend is calculated and what happens if the start year is moved. Ask whether the claim concerns a global average or a single location, and whether it concerns the surface or the whole energy budget. And notice whether a source distinguishes between what it knows well and what it does not, since willingness to specify uncertainty is the most reliable available marker of honest analysis in any technical field.

guides.title: Climate Models and Projections
guides.summary: How climate models are built, from the physical equations and grid discretisation through parameterisation, coupling and tuning, and how to read the projections they produce, including scenarios, ensembles, sensitivity, the track record and the genuine limits.

sections.heading: What a Climate Model Is, and What It Is Not
sections.body:
A climate model is a computer program that solves the equations of fluid motion, thermodynamics and radiation on
a three-dimensional grid wrapped around the Earth, stepping forward in time to simulate the atmosphere, ocean,
land surface and ice. It is not a statistical extrapolation of past temperature records, and it is not a
curve fitted to the warming already observed. It is a physical simulation built from conservation of mass,
momentum and energy, the same equations used to forecast tomorrow's weather, integrated for decades or centuries
instead of days.

The distinction between a weather forecast and a climate projection is the single most misunderstood point in
the subject, and it is worth being precise. Weather forecasting is an initial-value problem: given today's
observed state of the atmosphere, predict its specific state next Tuesday. Because the atmosphere is chaotic,
tiny errors in the initial state amplify, and useful deterministic skill is lost after roughly ten to fourteen
days. Climate projection is a boundary-value problem: given the amount of energy entering and leaving the
system, predict the statistics of the weather, its averages, its variability and its extremes, over decades. The
analogy often used is that nobody can tell you the temperature in Chicago on 14 March 2071, but everyone can
tell you that July in Chicago will be warmer than January, because that conclusion follows from the boundary
conditions rather than from the initial state. A climate model does not need to track individual storms
correctly to get the statistics of storms right.

What models produce is called a projection, deliberately not a prediction. A prediction says what will happen. A
projection says what will happen conditional on an assumption about future emissions, land use, population and
technology, none of which are governed by physics. Every credible climate figure carries a scenario label for
this reason. Reporting a projected warming without its scenario is like reporting a journey's arrival time
without saying the assumed speed.

The stakes justify the effort. Decisions worth trillions of currency units hang on these results: how high to
build a sea wall in Rotterdam, whether a farmer in the Sahel should switch cultivar, how a reinsurer should
price hurricane risk in Florida, what discount rate a treasury should apply to emissions reduction. Model output
also anchors international negotiation, since the Paris Agreement's targets of well below two degrees and
preferably one and a half degrees above pre-industrial temperature are stated in a currency that only models can
translate into emissions budgets.

Models are also the only laboratory available. There is exactly one Earth, no control planet, and no way to run
the twentieth century again without fossil fuels. A model is the closest thing to a controlled experiment the
science can have, which is both its great value and the source of the irreducible uncertainty that surrounds
every number it produces.

sections.heading: The Physical Foundations: Seven Equations and a Radiation Budget
sections.body:
Underneath every general circulation model sits a compact set of equations that have been known since the
nineteenth century. There are three momentum equations, one for each spatial direction, expressing Newton's
second law for a parcel of fluid on a rotating sphere; these are the Navier-Stokes equations with additional
Coriolis and gravitational terms. There is a continuity equation expressing conservation of mass. There is a
thermodynamic energy equation, the first law of thermodynamics applied to a moving parcel, including heating by
radiation, condensation and turbulent mixing. There is an equation of state, essentially the ideal gas law for
the atmosphere and a more complex empirical relation for seawater relating density to temperature, salinity and
pressure. And there is a conservation equation for water in its three phases. Vilhelm Bjerknes set out this
programme in 1904, arguing that weather prediction was in principle a problem of integrating these equations
from observed initial conditions.

The engine driving all of it is the radiation budget. The Sun delivers energy at an average of about 340 watts
per square metre averaged over the whole Earth's surface, derived from a solar constant near 1361 watts per
square metre divided by four, since a sphere intercepts sunlight over its cross-section but radiates from its
whole area. About thirty percent, roughly 100 watts per square metre, is reflected straight back to space by
clouds, aerosols, ice and bright land, a quantity called the planetary albedo. The remaining 240 watts per
square metre is absorbed and must, at equilibrium, be balanced by outgoing infrared radiation.

If Earth had no atmosphere, radiating 240 watts per square metre would require a surface temperature of about
255 kelvin, or minus 18 degrees Celsius, by the Stefan-Boltzmann law that emitted flux equals sigma times
temperature to the fourth power, with sigma equal to 5.67 times ten to the minus eight watts per square metre
per kelvin to the fourth. The observed average surface temperature is about 288 kelvin, 15 degrees Celsius. The
33-kelvin difference is the natural greenhouse effect, produced because water vapour, carbon dioxide, methane,
nitrous oxide and ozone absorb outgoing infrared radiation and re-emit it in all directions, including
downwards, from progressively colder altitudes.

Adding greenhouse gas raises the altitude from which infrared escapes to space. Because the troposphere cools
with height at roughly 6.5 kelvin per kilometre, emitting from higher up means emitting from colder air, which
means emitting less, which means the planet temporarily absorbs more than it emits and must warm until balance
is restored. This is the mechanism, and a model represents it by solving the radiative transfer equation
explicitly through tens of atmospheric layers using absorption line data measured in laboratories.

sections.heading: From Continuous Equations to a Discrete Grid: The Dynamical Core
sections.body:
The equations of fluid motion are continuous, and a computer can only hold finitely many numbers. The step that
converts one into the other is discretisation, and the piece of code that does it is called the dynamical core.
The globe is divided into boxes. A typical CMIP6-generation model uses horizontal boxes roughly 100 kilometres
on a side, though the range across models runs from about 250 kilometres down to 25 kilometres, with 30 to 90
vertical levels in the atmosphere from the surface to the mesosphere, and 40 to 75 levels in the ocean, which is
usually run at finer horizontal resolution, often 25 to 100 kilometres, because ocean eddies are smaller than
atmospheric ones.

Within each box the model carries a single value for each prognostic variable: temperature, the three components
of wind, pressure, humidity, and in the ocean salinity and current velocity. The model then advances all of them
by one time step, typically fifteen to thirty minutes for the atmosphere, using finite difference, finite volume
or spectral methods. The time step cannot be chosen freely. The Courant-Friedrichs-Lewy condition, published in
1928, requires that information must not travel more than one grid box per time step or the numerical scheme
becomes unstable and blows up. Halving the grid spacing therefore also requires halving the time step, so
doubling resolution in all three spatial dimensions plus time increases computational cost roughly sixteen-fold.
This single fact explains why climate model resolution has improved so slowly despite enormous growth in
computing power.

Spherical geometry introduces its own difficulty. A simple latitude-longitude grid has boxes that converge to
zero width at the poles, forcing impossibly short time steps there. Solutions include filtering the polar
regions, using a spectral representation in terms of spherical harmonics, as the European Centre's model does,
using a cubed-sphere grid that maps a cube onto the sphere, or using icosahedral and hexagonal meshes.

The dynamical core is the part of a climate model that is essentially settled science. Different cores, given
the same inputs, produce closely similar large-scale circulations, and their errors are well characterised. A
modern core conserves mass to machine precision and energy to within a fraction of a watt per square metre,
which matters enormously because the entire anthropogenic forcing being simulated is only about 2.7 watts per
square metre. A model with a spurious energy leak of one watt per square metre would be useless. Achieving that
conservation is a substantial engineering achievement and one of the reasons climate models are among the larger
scientific codebases in existence, commonly a million lines or more, developed over decades by teams of dozens.
Much of that code is still Fortran, not from inertia alone but because decades of numerical libraries and
validated physics routines are written in it, and rewriting a validated scheme risks introducing errors that
would be extremely hard to detect in a system whose output cannot be checked against a known answer.

sections.heading: Parameterisation: Representing the Physics Too Small to Resolve
sections.body:
A grid box 100 kilometres across cannot represent a cumulus cloud two kilometres wide, a thunderstorm updraught
one kilometre across, a turbulent eddy in the boundary layer ten metres across, or a breaking gravity wave over
a mountain ridge. Yet all of these move enormous quantities of heat, moisture and momentum, and a model that
ignored them would be badly wrong. The solution is parameterisation: for each unresolved process, write a rule
that predicts its aggregate effect on a grid box from the variables the model does carry.

Consider moist convection. The model knows a grid box's temperature and humidity profile. A convection scheme
asks whether that profile is unstable, meaning a lifted parcel would become buoyant, and if so how much mass
should be transported upwards, how much rain should fall out, and how much the surrounding air should warm by
compensating subsidence. The classic mass-flux approach, developed by Akio Arakawa and Wayne Schubert in 1974,
represents an ensemble of cumulus clouds by a spectrum of entraining plumes and closes the problem by assuming
the convection consumes instability at the rate the large-scale flow generates it. Every step involves choices
that are physically motivated but not uniquely determined.

Other major parameterisations cover boundary layer turbulence, cloud microphysics governing how droplets grow
and freeze, radiative transfer through a partly cloudy sky, gravity wave drag from flow over mountains, land
surface processes including soil moisture and vegetation, sea ice thermodynamics, aerosol formation and
deposition, and ocean mixing by eddies and internal waves. A modern model contains perhaps a dozen major
schemes, each with somewhere between five and fifty adjustable parameters, giving several hundred tunable
numbers in total.

This is where scientific judgement genuinely enters, and it is honest to say so plainly. The dynamical core is
constrained by physics that admits no argument; the parameterisations are constrained by physics plus
observations plus reasoned choice. Different modelling centres make different choices, which is precisely why
different models give different answers, and why the community deliberately maintains many independent models
rather than converging on one.

The frontier is eliminating the worst of these approximations by brute force. Global storm-resolving models
running at 1 to 5 kilometre grid spacing, such as those in the DYAMOND intercomparison, resolve deep convection
explicitly rather than parameterising it, removing what is arguably the single largest source of structural
error. They are extraordinarily expensive, currently affordable only for simulations of weeks to a year, and
they still parameterise turbulence and microphysics. A second frontier uses machine learning to emulate
high-resolution physics inside a coarse model, an approach that shows real promise but raises hard questions
about whether a data-trained scheme can be trusted to behave sensibly in a climate warmer than any it was
trained on.

sections.heading: Clouds: The Largest Single Source of Uncertainty
sections.body:
If one had to name the reason climate projections have an irreducible spread, the answer for the past forty
years has been clouds, and it remains largely true today. Clouds do two opposing things. They are bright, so
they reflect sunlight back to space and cool the planet, an effect worth roughly minus 45 watts per square metre
globally. They are also made of water, so they absorb and re-emit infrared radiation and warm the surface, worth
roughly plus 27 watts per square metre. The net effect today is a cooling of about 18 watts per square metre,
which is more than six times larger than the entire greenhouse forcing from human activity. A change of just a
few percent in that balance is therefore comparable to everything else in the problem.

Which effect dominates depends on cloud altitude and thickness. Low, thick marine stratocumulus decks, the grey
sheets that sit off the coasts of California, Peru and Namibia, are near the surface, so their tops are almost
as warm as the ocean below and they emit nearly as much infrared as the surface would; but they are bright, so
they reflect strongly. Their net effect is strong cooling. High, thin cirrus is the reverse: it is cold, so it
emits little infrared to space, trapping heat, and it is thin, so it reflects little sunlight. Its net effect is
warming.

The question that matters for projection is what happens to these clouds as the world warms, which is a
feedback rather than a forcing. If low cloud cover decreases with warming, more sunlight is absorbed, and
warming amplifies. If it increases, warming is damped. Models disagree, and they disagree most about exactly the
low marine clouds that matter most. The disagreement is not carelessness: these clouds are hundreds of metres
deep, sit in a delicate balance between surface evaporation, turbulent entrainment of dry air from above, and
radiative cooling at cloud top, and all of those processes are sub-grid scale.

Evidence has shifted somewhat towards a positive, that is amplifying, low-cloud feedback. Large-eddy simulations
resolving individual cloud layers at metre scale, satellite observations of how cloud cover responds to natural
temperature variations, and analysis of the relationship between cloud amount and estimated inversion strength
all point the same way. The IPCC Sixth Assessment Report in 2021 assessed the net cloud feedback as positive,
with a central estimate near plus 0.42 watts per square metre per kelvin, though with an assessed range spanning
roughly minus 0.10 to plus 0.94, still wide enough to matter. There is also a live and unresolved debate about
whether stratocumulus decks could break up abruptly at very high carbon dioxide levels, a possible discontinuity
suggested by high-resolution simulation but far from established.

sections.heading: Earth System Models: Coupling Ocean, Ice, Land and Carbon
sections.body:
An atmosphere alone cannot simulate climate change, because most of the heat and most of the memory of the
system live elsewhere. Over ninety percent of the extra energy trapped by greenhouse gases since 1970 has gone
into the ocean, not the air. Coupling an atmospheric model to an ocean model was therefore the decisive step,
achieved first by Syukuro Manabe and Kirk Bryan at Princeton in 1969, and it remains the defining feature of a
general circulation model.

Coupling is technically awkward because the components have wildly different timescales. The atmosphere adjusts
in days; the ocean mixed layer in months; the deep ocean in centuries to millennia; ice sheets in millennia. A
coupler component exchanges fluxes of heat, moisture, momentum, freshwater and carbon between components,
typically once per simulated hour or day, conserving each quantity exactly across the interface. Early coupled
models suffered from climate drift, in which small flux imbalances at the interface caused the simulated climate
to wander away from reality, and were patched with artificial flux adjustments. Those adjustments were widely
and fairly criticised as fudging; their elimination during the late 1990s and 2000s, achieved by improving the
components rather than correcting their output, was a genuine milestone in the field's credibility.

Modern models add sea ice with explicit thermodynamics and drift dynamics, land surface schemes carrying soil
moisture in multiple layers, snow, rivers and dynamic vegetation, and increasingly the biogeochemistry that
turns a climate model into an Earth system model. The carbon cycle is the important addition. Roughly half of
the carbon dioxide humans emit is currently absorbed by the ocean and by land plants; the rest accumulates.
Whether those sinks strengthen or weaken as the world warms is a first-order question, and only a model with an
interactive carbon cycle can address it. Most such models show sinks weakening under warming, adding an
amplifying feedback of a few tenths of a degree by 2100, but the spread across models for this quantity is
proportionally larger than for almost anything else.

Further components appear in the most complete models: interactive atmospheric chemistry for ozone and methane,
prognostic aerosols, permafrost carbon, ice sheet dynamics, and nitrogen limitation on plant growth, which turns
out to significantly restrain the carbon dioxide fertilisation effect that earlier models may have overstated.
Each addition makes a model more complete and also more uncertain, because it introduces new poorly constrained
processes. There is a real and healthy tension in the field between comprehensiveness and tractability, and
some researchers argue persuasively that simpler models, run in large ensembles, buy more understanding per unit
of computer time than the most elaborate ones. A hierarchy of models, from energy balance calculations on a
single page through intermediate complexity models to full Earth system models, is the practical compromise, and
understanding usually comes from comparing across that hierarchy rather than from any single rung of it.

sections.heading: A Short History: From Arrhenius to the CMIP Archives
sections.body:
The intellectual chain is longer than most people expect. Joseph Fourier reasoned in 1824 that the atmosphere
must retain heat, since a bare rock at Earth's distance from the Sun would be far colder than observed. John
Tyndall measured the infrared absorption of gases in his laboratory in 1859, establishing that water vapour and
carbon dioxide absorb heat radiation while nitrogen and oxygen do not. Svante Arrhenius, working by hand through
the winter of 1895 to 1896, performed the first quantitative calculation of the effect of doubling carbon
dioxide, obtaining roughly 5 to 6 degrees Celsius of warming, high by modern standards but astonishingly close
in kind. Guy Callendar assembled temperature records in 1938 and argued warming was already detectable.

Computing changed everything. In 1922 Lewis Fry Richardson published a hand-computed weather forecast that
failed spectacularly, for reasons later understood to involve unfiltered noise in the initial data, and imagined
a hall of 64,000 human computers producing forecasts in real time. In 1950 Jule Charney, Ragnar Fjørtoft and
John von Neumann ran the first numerical weather forecast on the ENIAC machine at Princeton. Norman Phillips
produced the first general circulation experiment in 1956, a two-layer model on a beta-plane that spontaneously
generated realistic mid-latitude weather systems.

Syukuro Manabe and Richard Wetherald published in 1967 the calculation that established the modern number: a
one-dimensional radiative-convective model that fixed relative humidity and allowed convection to set the lapse
rate, giving about 2.3 degrees Celsius of warming for doubled carbon dioxide. Manabe shared the 2021 Nobel Prize
in Physics for this line of work, with Klaus Hasselmann, who developed the fingerprinting methods used to
attribute observed change to causes, and Giorgio Parisi. In 1979 the United States National Academy of Sciences
convened a panel chaired by Jule Charney, which examined the two available models, Manabe's and James Hansen's,
added judgement, and concluded that doubling carbon dioxide would warm the planet by 1.5 to 4.5 degrees Celsius.
That range proved extraordinarily durable, essentially unchanged in official assessments for the next four
decades.

The modern era is defined by coordinated intercomparison. The Coupled Model Intercomparison Project began in
1995 and now runs in numbered phases: CMIP3 underpinned the IPCC's Fourth Assessment in 2007, CMIP5 the Fifth in
2013, and CMIP6 the Sixth in 2021, with over one hundred models from more than fifty institutions running a
standard protocol of experiments so that results can be compared directly. The output archive runs to tens of
petabytes and is freely available, which is the reason independent researchers can and do check the results
rather than taking them on trust. That openness is itself a deliberate response to criticism: the standard
protocol means every model answers the same question in the same way, so disagreements between centres cannot be
hidden behind differences in experimental design, and any competent outsider can download the raw fields and
recompute a published figure from scratch.

sections.heading: Spin-Up and Tuning: What It Is, and What It Is Not
sections.body:
Before a model can be used it must be brought into equilibrium, a process called spin-up. Starting from observed
temperature and salinity fields, the coupled system is run with fixed pre-industrial conditions, typically the
carbon dioxide concentration of 1850, roughly 285 parts per million, until the drift in global temperature and
in ocean heat content falls below an acceptable threshold. Because the deep ocean equilibrates over millennia,
spin-up runs commonly last five hundred to several thousand simulated years and consume a large share of a
project's total computer time before a single useful experiment has been run.

Tuning is the more contested word, and it deserves an honest account because it is routinely both understated by
advocates and grossly overstated by critics. Every parameterisation contains parameters whose values are not
precisely known from theory or measurement: the entrainment rate of cumulus plumes, the autoconversion threshold
at which cloud droplets become raindrops, the mixing length in the boundary layer, the fall speed of ice
crystals. Each has a physically plausible range, sometimes spanning a factor of two or more. Modellers choose
values within those ranges so that the simulated climate reproduces observed large-scale quantities.

The primary target is almost always the top-of-atmosphere radiation balance, which must come out close to zero
for a pre-industrial run, because a model with a persistent imbalance of even half a watt per square metre will
drift steadily away from a realistic state. Other common targets include the global mean surface temperature,
the distribution of sea ice, the strength of the jet streams, and the seasonal cycle of precipitation.

The crucial question is what is not tuned. It has become standard practice, and is now explicitly documented by
most centres, that models are not tuned to reproduce the observed twentieth-century warming trend, and are not
tuned to any particular value of climate sensitivity. This matters because if they were, the agreement between
simulated and observed warming would be circular and worthless as evidence. A 2017 survey of modelling groups by
Frédéric Hourdin and colleagues found that a minority of groups did consider twentieth-century warming during
development, and the community response was to insist on much greater transparency about tuning procedures, now
a required part of model documentation.

The honest summary is this: tuning is real, it is unavoidable, it is a legitimate part of building any complex
physical model, and it does not have enough free parameters to manufacture an arbitrary answer. A model has
several hundred tunable numbers and must simultaneously reproduce thousands of independent observed fields, from
the vertical structure of the tropical atmosphere to the seasonal cycle of Arctic sea ice to the location of the
intertropical convergence zone. The system is heavily overdetermined. But the existence of tuning is a genuine
reason that models are not fully independent of one another, which matters when interpreting how much agreement
between models really means.

sections.heading: Evaluating a Model: Hindcasts, Reanalyses and Out-of-Sample Tests
sections.body:
A model's credibility rests on tests it could have failed. The weakest test, and the one most often cited by
non-specialists, is whether a model reproduces the observed warming curve. It is weak precisely because the
result was known in advance to the modellers. Stronger tests come in several forms.

The first is reproduction of the mean state and its seasonal cycle across many variables that were never
targeted: the position and strength of the Hadley circulation, the monsoons, the storm tracks, the vertical
temperature structure, the ocean's meridional overturning. Comparison is made against reanalyses, which are
observational datasets produced by assimilating decades of measurements into a weather model to give a
physically consistent gridded history. ERA5 from the European Centre, covering 1940 onwards, is the current
standard. Reanalyses are not pure observation and carry their own model-derived errors, a subtlety often
forgotten.

The second is reproduction of natural variability the model was never shown: the El Niño Southern Oscillation
with its two to seven year period, the Madden-Julian Oscillation, the quasi-biennial oscillation of tropical
stratospheric winds, the North Atlantic Oscillation. Models have improved markedly here, and the fact that a
model spontaneously generates an El Niño with roughly the right period and spatial pattern from physics alone is
strong evidence that it captures the relevant coupled dynamics, though amplitude and asymmetry errors persist.

The third and most convincing is out-of-sample prediction of events that had not happened when the model was
built. The eruption of Mount Pinatubo in June 1991 injected about 20 million tonnes of sulphur dioxide into the
stratosphere. James Hansen's group published a forecast within months that global temperature would fall by
roughly 0.5 degrees Celsius and then recover over several years. It did. Similar successful out-of-sample
predictions include stratospheric cooling as a fingerprint distinguishing greenhouse warming from solar
brightening, since more sunlight would warm the stratosphere while more carbon dioxide cools it, and the
observed cooling is unambiguous; polar amplification, with the Arctic warming two to four times the global rate;
and the intensification of the water cycle, wet regions getting wetter and dry drier over the ocean.

Models also fail visibly, and cataloguing the failures is part of the discipline. The persistent double
intertropical convergence zone, in which most models generate a spurious second rain band south of the equator
in the Pacific, has resisted correction for thirty years. Precipitation over complex terrain, the Southern Ocean
radiation balance, Antarctic sea ice trends, and the frequency of atmospheric blocking are all known problem
areas. A responsible reader should ask, for any given projected quantity, whether models demonstrate skill for
that quantity specifically, not merely for global temperature.

sections.heading: Climate Sensitivity: The Number Everything Depends On
sections.body:
If one number summarises a climate model's implications, it is the equilibrium climate sensitivity, or ECS: the
global mean surface warming that eventually results from doubling the pre-industrial carbon dioxide
concentration, once the system has fully equilibrated. A closely related and more policy-relevant quantity is
the transient climate response, or TCR: the warming at the moment of doubling in an idealised experiment where
carbon dioxide rises at one percent per year, reaching doubling after seventy years. TCR is smaller than ECS
because the ocean is still absorbing heat and has not caught up.

The physics decomposes cleanly. Doubling carbon dioxide produces a radiative forcing of about 3.9 watts per
square metre, a figure calculated from line-by-line radiative transfer and known to within a few percent. With
no feedbacks at all, the Planck response alone, meaning simply that a warmer planet radiates more, would give
about 1.2 degrees Celsius of warming. Feedbacks then amplify this. Water vapour is the largest: warmer air holds
more moisture, roughly seven percent more per degree by the Clausius-Clapeyron relation, and water vapour is a
greenhouse gas, contributing roughly plus 1.3 watts per square metre per kelvin. The lapse rate feedback is
negative, around minus 0.5, because warming is amplified aloft in the tropics. Surface albedo feedback from
melting ice and snow adds about plus 0.3. Cloud feedback adds the contested plus 0.42 or thereabouts. Summing
gives a net feedback that leaves ECS in the region of 3 degrees.

The assessed range has a long history of stubbornness. The Charney report gave 1.5 to 4.5 degrees in 1979, and
the IPCC repeated essentially that range through its Fifth Assessment in 2013. The Sixth Assessment in 2021
narrowed it materially for the first time, giving a best estimate of 3 degrees Celsius with a likely range of
2.5 to 4 and a very likely range of 2 to 5. That narrowing came not from models alone but from combining three
independent lines of evidence: process understanding of individual feedbacks, the historical warming record, and
paleoclimate constraints from the Last Glacial Maximum and past warm periods.

The narrowing had to be done carefully because of the so-called hot model problem. A subset of CMIP6 models,
perhaps a fifth of them, produced ECS values above 5 degrees, considerably higher than CMIP5, largely through
changes in cloud microphysics parameterisations. Independent evidence, particularly paleoclimate and the
historical record, indicates these high values are unlikely. The IPCC therefore did not take a simple average of
models, instead weighting projections by assessed sensitivity, a methodological shift with real consequences.
It is a good illustration that the models are an input to expert assessment, not the final word.

sections.heading: Scenarios: The Human Assumptions Inside Every Projection
sections.body:
A model cannot know how much carbon dioxide humanity will emit, because that depends on politics, technology,
demography and economics. Projections are therefore always conditional, and the condition is called a scenario.
Understanding the scenario framework is essential to reading any climate figure correctly, and misuse of
scenarios is probably the most common serious error in public discussion of climate projections.

The frameworks have evolved. The IPCC's Special Report on Emissions Scenarios of 2000 produced the SRES
families, labelled A1, A2, B1, B2 and variants. These were replaced for the Fifth Assessment by the
Representative Concentration Pathways, named for the radiative forcing they reach in 2100 in watts per square
metre: RCP2.6, RCP4.5, RCP6.0 and RCP8.5. The Sixth Assessment adopted the Shared Socioeconomic Pathways, which
pair a narrative about how the world develops with a forcing level, giving labels such as SSP1-1.9, SSP1-2.6,
SSP2-4.5, SSP3-7.0 and SSP5-8.5. The number after the hyphen is still the 2100 forcing.

Roughly, and using the IPCC Sixth Assessment's own figures for warming in 2081 to 2100 relative to 1850 to 1900:
SSP1-1.9 gives about 1.4 degrees Celsius and is the only pathway broadly consistent with the 1.5 degree Paris
aspiration; SSP1-2.6 gives about 1.8; SSP2-4.5, often described as a middle-of-the-road continuation of current
policies and pledges, gives about 2.7; SSP3-7.0 gives about 3.6; and SSP5-8.5, a fossil-fuel-intensive future,
gives about 4.4, with a very likely range extending above 5.

The status of the highest scenario is genuinely contested and worth stating carefully. RCP8.5 and SSP5-8.5 were
designed as high-end reference cases, not as best-guess business-as-usual, and they assume a very large
expansion of coal use through the century that now looks implausible given the collapse in solar and wind costs.
Many researchers, notably Zeke Hausfather and Glen Peters in a widely cited 2020 commentary, argue that using
RCP8.5 as business-as-usual is misleading and has distorted both public perception and the impacts literature.
Others counter that high-end scenarios remain useful for stress-testing, especially because carbon cycle
feedbacks could push concentrations higher than emissions alone imply. The defensible position is that SSP2-4.5
and SSP3-7.0 currently bracket plausible no-further-action outcomes, and SSP5-8.5 should be labelled explicitly
as a low-probability high-end case rather than as what will happen.

The practical consequence for a reader is simple and strict. A projected impact number without a scenario is
uninterpretable. Two studies of the same city's flood risk can differ by a factor of three purely because one
used SSP1-2.6 and the other SSP5-8.5, with no disagreement about physics whatsoever.

It is also worth understanding that scenarios enter a model in one of two ways. In concentration-driven runs,
which are the majority, the modeller specifies atmospheric greenhouse gas concentrations directly and the model
computes the climate response. In emissions-driven runs, the modeller specifies emissions and the model's
interactive carbon cycle determines the resulting concentrations, which allows carbon cycle feedbacks to affect
the answer but introduces additional spread. The two approaches can give noticeably different warming for the
nominally identical scenario, and comparisons across studies should check which was used.

sections.heading: Ensembles and the Three Distinct Sources of Uncertainty
sections.body:
No serious projection is made with one model run. Instead, ensembles are used, and different kinds of ensemble
isolate different sources of uncertainty. Distinguishing the three sources is what allows a projection's spread
to be interpreted rather than merely reported.

The first source is internal variability, the natural chaotic fluctuation of the climate system that would occur
even with constant forcing. To quantify it, a single model is run many times from very slightly different
initial conditions, a perturbation as small as a rounding-level change in one grid point's temperature. Because
the system is chaotic these runs diverge into different sequences of El Niño events, different decadal ocean
patterns, and different regional trends. Large initial-condition ensembles, such as the 40-member Community
Earth System Model ensemble, reveal that regional trends over twenty to thirty years can differ substantially
between members purely by chance. This is a fundamental limit: no improvement in models can remove it, because
it reflects real unpredictability in the system rather than ignorance.

The second source is model uncertainty, meaning structural differences between models built by different teams
making different defensible choices. This is quantified by multi-model ensembles such as CMIP6. It is reducible
in principle by better physics and higher resolution, and has narrowed slowly over decades.

The third is scenario uncertainty, which is not scientific uncertainty at all but uncertainty about human
choices, quantified by running the same models under several SSPs.

Their relative importance shifts systematically with time horizon and spatial scale, a result established by Ed
Hawkins and Rowan Sutton in 2009 that every practitioner should know. For global temperature over the next
decade or two, internal variability and model uncertainty dominate and scenario choice barely matters, because
the emissions pathways have not yet diverged much. By the end of the century, scenario uncertainty dominates
overwhelmingly. For regional precipitation, internal variability remains a large fraction of the total even at
long horizons. The implication is directly practical: for near-term adaptation planning, arguing about emissions
scenarios is largely beside the point, whereas for long-lived infrastructure the scenario is the dominant
question.

A subtlety that deserves flagging is that multi-model ensembles are not statistically clean samples. Models
share code, share parameterisation schemes, share intellectual lineage, and are sometimes literally descended
from one another. The spread across an ensemble is therefore not a probability distribution in any rigorous
sense, and treating the model mean as a best estimate and the spread as a confidence interval is a convenient
convention rather than a defensible statistical procedure. Weighting models by demonstrated skill, or accounting
for shared lineage, is an active research area.

One further point often causes confusion. Averaging many model runs together smooths out internal variability,
which is exactly what you want when isolating the forced signal, but it also smooths out extremes and produces a
picture that is unrealistically calm. A multi-model mean temperature series looks far steadier than any real
climate will be. Real futures will contain pauses, spikes and record-breaking years embedded in the trend, and
mistaking the smoothness of an ensemble mean for a prediction of smooth change is a persistent error.

sections.heading: Downscaling: Getting From a Global Grid to a Local Decision
sections.body:
A global model with 100-kilometre grid boxes cannot tell a water utility what will happen to a particular
catchment, because the catchment may be smaller than one grid box and its rainfall may be governed by terrain
the model represents as a smooth bump. Bridging that gap is called downscaling, and it is where most practical
climate information is actually produced. It is also where the most errors are made, because downscaling can add
apparent precision without adding real information.

There are two families of method. Dynamical downscaling nests a regional climate model, typically at 4 to 25
kilometre resolution, inside the global model, taking boundary conditions from the global run and solving the
same physical equations at finer scale over a limited area. It resolves mountains, coastlines and lake effects
properly and can generate physically consistent extremes, but it is expensive and it inherits every error in the
global model that supplies its boundaries. Coordinated efforts such as CORDEX provide standardised regional
downscaling for every continent.

Statistical downscaling instead builds an empirical relationship between large-scale variables the global model
simulates well and local variables of interest, using observed historical data, then applies that relationship
to the projected future. It is cheap enough to apply to dozens of models and scenarios, which is a decisive
practical advantage. Its central weakness is the stationarity assumption: it presumes the historical statistical
relationship still holds in a changed climate, which cannot be verified and may fail exactly when it matters.
steps: Define the decision first, not the data. Establish which variable, at which threshold, over which averaging period, actually changes what you would do. A reservoir operator may need consecutive dry days above a specific count; a bridge designer needs a rainfall intensity for a stated return period. Vague requests produce useless downscaling.
Choose the time horizon and match it to the asset's lifetime, and recognise that for horizons under about thirty years internal variability will usually dominate the signal.

Select an ensemble of global models rather than one, and check whether the chosen models simulate the relevant regional processes with any demonstrated skill. Discard models with gross errors in the phenomenon you care about, and document why.
Select scenarios that bracket the plausible range, typically a strong-mitigation and a high-emissions case, and always report results separately for each rather than averaging across them.

Apply bias correction against a local observational record of at least thirty years, using quantile mapping or a similar method, and be explicit that bias correction cannot repair a model that gets the underlying process wrong.
Quantify and report the spread, not just the central estimate, separating internal variability from model spread where the ensemble design allows it.

Stress-test the decision against the full range rather than optimising for the central estimate, and prefer options that perform acceptably across all of it, an approach known as robust decision making.
Document every choice, including models discarded and why, so the analysis can be reproduced and revisited as new model generations appear.

sections.heading: The Track Record: What Models Got Right and What They Missed
sections.body:
Because climate projections have now been made for over fifty years, their performance can be assessed rather
than merely asserted. This is the most valuable evidence available about model reliability, and it is mixed in
an instructive way.

The clearest test is global mean surface temperature. A 2019 study by Zeke Hausfather, Henri Drake, Tristan
Abbott and Gavin Schmidt evaluated seventeen projections published between 1970 and 2007, comparing each against
subsequent observations. Crucially, they distinguished two questions: did the model project the right warming
for the time period, and did it project the right warming per unit of forcing? The second question is the fair
test of the physics, because a model given the wrong future emissions cannot be blamed for the resulting error.
Fourteen of the seventeen were consistent with observations on the implied warming-per-forcing measure, and ten
of the seventeen were consistent even on raw projected temperature. James Hansen's 1988 projections ran warm on
raw temperature, but principally because the emissions scenario assumed continued rapid growth in
chlorofluorocarbons that the Montreal Protocol of 1987 prevented; corrected for actual forcing, the physics
held up well.

Several structural predictions have been confirmed, and these carry more evidential weight than the temperature
curve because they are qualitative fingerprints that competing explanations do not produce. The stratosphere has
cooled sharply while the troposphere warmed, which greenhouse gases predict and increased solar output would
not. Nights have warmed faster than days. Winters have warmed faster than summers. The Arctic has warmed roughly
three times the global rate. Sea level has risen and is accelerating. The tropopause has risen. Atmospheric
water vapour has increased at close to the predicted seven percent per degree.

There are also significant misses, and honest accounting requires naming them. Models substantially
underestimated the rate of Arctic sea ice decline in September, which fell faster than nearly all CMIP3 and
CMIP5 models projected. Ice sheet contributions to sea level rise were underestimated in earlier assessments,
largely because dynamic ice loss processes such as marine ice cliff instability and ice shelf buttressing were
not represented at all rather than represented badly. Antarctic sea ice, which expanded slightly until 2015 and
then dropped abruptly, is not well simulated by any model. Some extreme heat events, notably the Pacific
Northwest heat dome of June 2021 which exceeded the previous record in Lytton, British Columbia by nearly five
degrees Celsius, have been far outside what models suggested was possible, raising an unresolved question about
whether models underestimate the tail of the distribution.

The overall pattern is that models have been reliable for large-scale thermodynamic quantities and less reliable
for dynamical and cryospheric ones, and where they have erred on impacts they have more often erred towards
understatement than overstatement.

sections.heading: Tipping Points and Deep Uncertainty: The Limits of the Method
sections.body:
Some of the most consequential possibilities in the climate system are precisely those a conventional model
handles worst. A tipping element is a component with self-reinforcing feedbacks strong enough that, past some
threshold, it transitions to a qualitatively different state and does not return when the forcing is removed.
The candidate list, developed by Timothy Lenton and colleagues since 2008 and updated in 2022, includes the
Greenland and West Antarctic ice sheets, the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation, Amazon forest dieback,
permafrost carbon release, boreal forest shifts, and low-latitude coral reefs.

Models handle these badly for structural reasons. Ice sheet models are only now being coupled interactively into
Earth system models rather than run offline, and the processes that could cause rapid collapse operate at
grounding lines a few hundred metres across, far below any global grid. The Atlantic overturning circulation
weakens in most model projections but abrupt collapse this century is projected by few of them, while
paleoclimate records show it has collapsed and restarted repeatedly in the past, and some observational analyses
suggest it is closer to a threshold than models indicate. This is a genuine and unresolved tension between
different lines of evidence, and anyone claiming certainty in either direction is overstating the case.

The deeper issue is that models are calibrated on the observed climate, and a tipping point is by definition a
departure from the regime in which they were calibrated. A model can be excellent at interpolation and poor at
extrapolation without any way to tell from its performance on historical data. This is a species of uncertainty
often called deep uncertainty, meaning that the probability distribution itself is unknown, not merely wide.

Three further limits deserve honest statement. First, models cannot forecast human behaviour, so they cannot
predict emissions, and the scenario spread is not a probability distribution over futures. Second, models say
little useful about the compounding of climate impacts with social systems, since crop failure translates into
famine only through markets, governments and infrastructure that no climate model contains. Third, the tails of
the distribution, the low-probability high-impact outcomes that dominate risk-based reasoning, are exactly where
model evidence is thinnest, because rare events are undersampled and the processes that generate them are often
unresolved.

None of this undermines the central findings. That the planet is warming, that human emissions are the cause,
and that further emissions cause further warming are supported by evidence far broader than models, including
direct radiative measurements, paleoclimate, and simple energy balance arguments. But it does mean that the
precise numbers deserve to be held with appropriate humility, particularly for regional and extreme outcomes.
The appropriate response to deep uncertainty is not paralysis and not false precision, but decision frameworks
that seek options performing tolerably across the whole range of plausible futures rather than optimally in the
single most likely one.

sections.heading: Reading a Projection Responsibly: A Practical Checklist
sections.body:
Most people encounter climate models through a headline number, and most such numbers are misread in
identifiable ways. A few habits protect against nearly all of them.

Always find the scenario. A figure without one is meaningless, and if the source does not state it, treat the
number as unreliable until you can establish it. Then ask whether that scenario is being presented honestly. If
the number comes from SSP5-8.5 or RCP8.5 and is described as business-as-usual or as what will happen, the
framing is questionable, and comparing it with a number derived from SSP2-4.5 is comparing different questions.

Always find the baseline. Warming figures may be quoted relative to 1850 to 1900, which the IPCC uses as a proxy
for pre-industrial, relative to the 1961 to 1990 or 1986 to 2005 averages, or relative to the present. Since
roughly 1.1 to 1.3 degrees Celsius of warming has already occurred, the choice of baseline shifts every number
by that much, and confusion between baselines accounts for a large share of apparent contradictions between
sources.

Always find the spread. A single number is a central estimate drawn from a distribution, and the width of that
distribution is frequently the more important fact. Note whether the range quoted is a likely range, meaning
IPCC's 66 percent probability, or a very likely range meaning 90 percent, since these differ substantially.

Ask what the quantity is averaged over. Global annual mean warming is a robust model output. Summer rainfall in
a single valley in 2043 is not, and the further you move from global and annual towards local and instantaneous,
the less model skill exists. Ask whether the specific quantity has demonstrated skill, not whether models in
general are good.

Prefer multi-model ensembles to single models, and be sceptical of any result resting on one model, especially
if that model is at the extreme of the sensitivity range. Prefer assessments such as the IPCC reports, which
weigh model output against observational and paleoclimate evidence, over raw model output.

When something appears to go wrong, that is, when a projection is contradicted by observation, work through the
diagnosis in order rather than concluding the models are broken. Check first whether the actual forcing matched
the assumed scenario, since most apparent failures are scenario errors. Check second whether the discrepancy
lies within the range of internal variability, which for a decade of regional trend is often large. Check third
whether the observational record itself has been revised, which happens routinely. Only after those three does
genuine model error become the leading explanation, and even then the useful question is which process is
misrepresented, since that is what improves the next generation.

guides.title: Climate Sensitivity and Radiative Forcing
guides.summary: How physicists measure the push humans apply to the climate system, in watts per square metre, and how much warming that push eventually produces. Covers the energy budget, the greenhouse mechanism, every major feedback, the three definitions of sensitivity, the evidence from instruments, paleoclimate and models, and why the remaining uncertainty is dominated by clouds.

sections.heading: Why One Number Frames the Whole Climate Problem
sections.body:
Almost every practical question about a warming planet collapses onto a single quantity. How hot will it get? How fast must emissions fall to hold a given target? How much damage is already committed? Each of these depends on the same underlying property of the Earth system: how strongly the surface temperature responds to a change in the planet's energy balance. Climate scientists call that property climate sensitivity, and in its most-quoted form it answers a deliberately artificial question. Suppose the carbon dioxide concentration of the atmosphere were doubled and then held fixed forever, and the planet were left alone for many centuries to settle into a new steady state. How much warmer would the global mean surface temperature be?

The answer is a temperature. The 2021 assessment by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change gave a best estimate of 3 degrees Celsius, a likely range of 2.5 to 4 degrees, and a very likely range of 2 to 5 degrees. Those numbers had barely moved in forty years, which is often reported as a failure of the science; it is better understood as the signature of a genuinely hard problem in which several independent lines of evidence agree with each other but none is sharp.

The leverage of this one number is enormous. If sensitivity is near 2 degrees, the carbon budget consistent with holding warming below 2 degrees is roughly twice as large as if sensitivity is near 4. Sea level rise, the fraction of the tropics that becomes uninhabitably humid on the wet-bulb measure, the probability of losing the Amazon or the West Antarctic ice sheet — all scale with it. A policy debate about how urgently to decarbonise is, underneath the rhetoric, largely a disagreement about where in that range the true value sits, plus a disagreement about how much weight to give to the upper tail.

The concept is old. The Swedish chemist Svante Arrhenius calculated in 1896, by hand, using infrared measurements of the Moon, that halving carbon dioxide would cool the Earth by 4 to 5 degrees and doubling it would warm the planet by a similar amount. His number was in the right range for substantially the wrong reasons, but the framing survived. The modern convention was fixed by a 1979 report chaired by the meteorologist Jule Charney for the United States National Academy of Sciences, which gave 1.5 to 4.5 degrees for a doubling. That range, sometimes called the Charney sensitivity, remained the official estimate for more than three decades.

To understand what the number means, and why it is hard to pin down, requires separating two distinct things: the size of the push applied to the climate, and the size of the system's response to that push. The first is called radiative forcing and is known fairly precisely. The second is where the difficulty lives.

sections.heading: The Planet's Energy Budget
sections.body:
Every question about global temperature begins with a simple accounting identity. Energy arrives at Earth almost entirely as sunlight and leaves almost entirely as infrared radiation. If more arrives than leaves, the planet accumulates heat and warms. If more leaves than arrives, it cools. If the two balance, temperature is steady. Nothing else in the budget matters at the global scale: geothermal heat from the Earth's interior contributes about 0.09 watts per square metre and human energy use about 0.03, against a solar input of roughly 340.

That solar figure deserves care because it is a frequent source of confusion. The solar constant, the flux of sunlight crossing a surface held perpendicular to the Sun's rays at Earth's mean orbital distance, is about 1,361 watts per square metre. But the Earth intercepts sunlight over a disc of area pi times the radius squared, while it radiates from a sphere of area four pi times the radius squared. The intercepted energy is therefore spread over four times the area, giving a global average incoming flux of 1,361 divided by 4, or roughly 340 watts per square metre.

Not all of that is absorbed. About 29 to 30 per cent is reflected straight back to space, mostly by clouds, partly by bright surfaces such as snow, ice, deserts and the ocean at grazing angles, and partly by scattering off air molecules and aerosol particles.
