That reflected fraction is the planetary albedo. Roughly 100 watts per square metre bounce off; about 240 are absorbed, a little under a quarter of that in the atmosphere itself and the rest at the surface.

To balance the books the Earth must radiate about 240 watts per square metre back to space as infrared. The Stefan–Boltzmann law states that a perfect radiator emits sigma times temperature to the fourth power, where sigma is 5.67 times ten to the minus eighth watts per square metre per kelvin to the fourth. Setting that equal to 240 gives an emission temperature of about 255 kelvin, or minus 18 degrees Celsius. The actual global mean surface temperature is about 15 degrees Celsius, some 33 degrees warmer. That 33-degree gap is the natural greenhouse effect, and it is the reason the planet has liquid oceans rather than being a frozen rock.

The crucial point for everything that follows is that the 255-kelvin emission temperature is not a surface temperature. It is the temperature of whatever layer actually does the radiating to space, which for the infrared bands that matter sits several kilometres up in the troposphere. The surface is warmer than the emitting layer because temperature falls with altitude. This is the hinge on which the entire greenhouse mechanism turns, and it explains why adding a gas that is transparent to sunlight but opaque to infrared changes the surface temperature at all.

sections.heading: Radiative Forcing: The Watt-per-Square-Metre Yardstick
sections.body:
Radiative forcing is the bookkeeping device that lets utterly different human and natural influences be compared on one scale. Its definition is precise and slightly counterintuitive: it is the change in the net downward energy flux at the top of the atmosphere, measured in watts per square metre, caused by some imposed change, with surface and tropospheric temperatures held fixed at their unperturbed values. A positive forcing means the planet is temporarily gaining energy and will warm; a negative forcing means it is losing energy and will cool.

The reason temperatures are held fixed in the definition is to separate cause from consequence. If you allowed the surface to warm while calculating the forcing, you would be mixing in the response, and the whole point of the exercise is to isolate the push so that the response can be studied separately. In practice the standard modern measure is effective radiative forcing, which allows the stratosphere and the atmosphere's clouds, water vapour and circulation to adjust rapidly while keeping the global mean surface temperature pinned. These fast adjustments happen on timescales of days to a few months and are physically distinct from the slow, temperature-mediated feedbacks that follow. The older measure, stratosphere-adjusted radiative forcing, allowed only the stratosphere to relax; for carbon dioxide the two are close, but for aerosols and black carbon they differ substantially, which is why the effective version is now preferred.

Once forcings are expressed this way they simply add. A forcing of plus 2 from greenhouse gases and minus 1 from aerosols gives a net of plus 1, and to a good approximation the system does not care which agents produced it. This additivity is an empirical result rather than a theorem, and it breaks down in places — the overlap between the infrared absorption bands of carbon dioxide, water vapour and methane means their combined effect is a little less than the sum of their separate effects, and models account for that explicitly — but as an organising principle it is remarkably robust.

The magnitudes are worth fixing in mind. Since 1750 the total effective radiative forcing from human activity is assessed at about 2.7 watts per square metre, with a likely range of roughly 2.0 to 3.4. Carbon dioxide alone accounts for about 2.2 of that. Methane contributes about 0.5 directly and more when its chemical effects on ozone and stratospheric water vapour are included. Aerosols offset a substantial and poorly constrained fraction, best estimated at about minus 1.1 watts per square metre. Changes in solar output over the same period contribute perhaps 0.01 to 0.1, an order of magnitude smaller than the greenhouse term and in the wrong direction to explain recent warming, since solar activity has drifted slightly downward since the 1980s while temperatures rose sharply.

sections.heading: How Trace Gases Trap Heat
sections.body:
The greenhouse mechanism is often described as gases acting like a blanket or like the glass of a greenhouse. Both analogies mislead. A real greenhouse works mainly by preventing convection: the glass stops warm air from rising away. Atmospheric greenhouse gases do something quite different, and understanding what requires thinking about where in the atmosphere radiation escapes to space.

Start with the physics of the molecules. Nitrogen and oxygen, which together make up 99 per cent of dry air, are diatomic molecules made of two identical atoms. They have no permanent electric dipole moment, and their vibrations do not create one, so they interact only very weakly with infrared radiation. Carbon dioxide, water vapour, methane, nitrous oxide and ozone are different. Carbon dioxide is linear and symmetric, so it too has no permanent dipole, but its bending mode — the vibration in which the molecule flexes out of a straight line — produces a transient dipole and absorbs strongly at a wavelength near 15 micrometres. That happens to sit close to the peak of the infrared emission of a body at terrestrial temperatures, which is why a gas present at only 0.04 per cent by volume matters so much. Water vapour absorbs across a broad set of bands from about 5 to 8 micrometres and again beyond 17. Methane absorbs near 7.7 micrometres. The gap between roughly 8 and 12 micrometres where absorption is weak is called the atmospheric window, and it is the main channel through which the surface radiates directly to space.

Now the mechanism. Infrared photons emitted by the surface in a strongly absorbed band do not escape. They are absorbed within metres or tens of metres, the absorbing molecule shares that energy with surrounding air by collision, and the air re-emits in all directions at the local temperature. Radiation escaping to space in that band therefore comes not from the surface but from an altitude high enough that the air above is thin enough to be transparent — the effective emission level. Because temperature in the troposphere falls with height at roughly 6.5 kelvin per kilometre, that emission level is colder than the surface, and a colder emitter radiates less.

Add more carbon dioxide and the effective emission level rises. At a higher, colder altitude the gas emits less energy to space in that band, so the planet's total outgoing radiation drops below the incoming 240 watts per square metre. The imbalance is the forcing. The planet then warms until the emission level, and everything below it, has heated enough to restore 240 watts per square metre of outgoing flux. This is why the mechanism is sometimes summarised as raising the radiating height, and why it depends absolutely on the atmosphere having a temperature that decreases with altitude. On a planet with an isothermal atmosphere, adding greenhouse gases would change nothing at all.

sections.heading: The Logarithmic Law and the Doubling Convention
sections.body:
Carbon dioxide's forcing does not grow in proportion to its concentration. It grows roughly in proportion to the logarithm of the concentration, which means each successive doubling adds about the same amount of forcing as the one before. Going from 280 to 560 parts per million produces the same push as going from 560 to 1,120. This single fact explains why the field expresses sensitivity per doubling rather than per part per million, and it has large practical consequences.

The standard formula, fitted to detailed line-by-line radiative transfer calculations, is that the forcing equals about 5.35 times the natural logarithm of the ratio of new to old concentration, in watts per square metre. A doubling gives 5.35 times the natural log of 2, or roughly 3.7. More recent work using improved spectroscopic databases and accounting for the way the forcing depends weakly on the background state gives a slightly higher figure: the current best estimate for a doubling of carbon dioxide from pre-industrial levels is 3.93 watts per square metre, with an uncertainty of about 12 per cent. That revision, published in 2016 by Gunnar Myhre and colleagues and confirmed since, nudged forcing-based sensitivity estimates downward by a few per cent because the same observed warming was now attributed to a slightly larger push.

The reason for the logarithm is spectroscopic. At the centre of the 15-micrometre band, the atmosphere is already so opaque that adding more gas changes nothing; the emission level there is already in the stratosphere. All the action happens in the wings of the band, where absorption is partial. Each spectral line has a shape with tails that fall off roughly as the inverse square of the distance from the line centre. As concentration rises, the wings become opaque outward from the centre, and the width of the saturated region grows only as the logarithm of concentration. That geometry — a line shape with power-law tails, saturating outward — is what generates the logarithmic law. It is not an assumption; it falls out of the pressure-broadened Lorentz line shape.

This is the grain of truth inside the common claim that carbon dioxide is saturated and further emissions cannot matter. The band centre genuinely is saturated. The wings are not, and the total absorption keeps growing without limit, merely slowly. Diminishing returns are not the same as no returns, and because emissions are cumulative and concentrations have been rising exponentially rather than linearly, the logarithm has so far been fed an exponential and has produced an approximately linear increase in forcing over time.

The convention carries a hazard worth naming. Because forcing is per doubling, statements about warming per doubling do not translate simply into warming per tonne emitted. The relationship between cumulative emissions and warming turns out to be close to linear for a separate reason involving the ocean's uptake of both carbon and heat, but that near-linearity is a coincidence of two offsetting curvatures rather than a fundamental law.

sections.heading: The Other Forcing Agents
sections.body:
Carbon dioxide dominates, but it is not alone, and several of the other agents matter enormously for the shape of the near-term problem.

Methane is the second largest greenhouse contributor. A molecule of methane absorbs infrared far more effectively than a molecule of carbon dioxide, and its concentration has risen from about 700 parts per billion pre-industrially to over 1,900 today. Its direct forcing is about 0.5 watts per square metre, rising to roughly 1.2 once indirect effects are counted: methane oxidises in the atmosphere to produce tropospheric ozone, itself a greenhouse gas, and stratospheric water vapour. Its crucial distinguishing feature is a lifetime of about twelve years, against centuries to millennia for the effective persistence of carbon dioxide. Cutting methane emissions therefore reduces forcing quickly, which is why methane control is emphasised as a lever on the next few decades specifically.

Nitrous oxide, largely from fertilised soils and manure, contributes about 0.2 watts per square metre and has a lifetime near 116 years. Halocarbons — the chlorofluorocarbons and their substitutes — contribute about 0.4, and are the one category where deliberate international regulation has already bent the curve, through the Montreal Protocol of 1987 and its Kigali Amendment.

Aerosols are the great counterweight and the great uncertainty. Sulphate particles from burning coal and oil, along with nitrates and some organic compounds, scatter sunlight directly back to space, a cooling effect of roughly minus 0.2 to minus 0.3 watts per square metre. Far larger, and far harder to quantify, is the indirect effect: aerosols act as cloud condensation nuclei, and more nuclei in a fixed amount of water produce more, smaller droplets, which makes clouds brighter and may make them longer-lived. The best estimate for the total aerosol effective radiative forcing is about minus 1.1 watts per square metre with a very likely range from about minus 1.7 to minus 0.4. That range is wide enough to be the single largest contributor to uncertainty in forcing-based sensitivity estimates, for a reason that is worth stating baldly: if aerosol cooling has been strongly masking greenhouse warming, then sensitivity must be high to explain the observed temperature record, and vice versa. Black carbon soot is the exception among aerosols, absorbing rather than scattering, and warms.

Land use change works mainly through albedo. Replacing dark boreal forest with pale cropland reflects more sunlight, a global forcing of about minus 0.2 watts per square metre, though in the tropics deforestation warms locally by suppressing evaporative cooling.

Natural forcings complete the picture. Large explosive volcanic eruptions inject sulphur dioxide into the stratosphere, where it forms a sulphate veil lasting one to three years; Pinatubo in 1991 produced a peak forcing near minus 3 watts per square metre and cooled the planet by about 0.4 degrees. Solar variation over the eleven-year cycle amounts to about 0.1 per cent of total output, roughly 0.2 watts per square metre of forcing peak to trough.

sections.heading: The Planck Response: The Restoring Force
sections.body:
If the climate had no feedbacks at all, sensitivity would be a straightforward calculation from the Stefan–Boltzmann law, and the answer would be reassuringly small. Understanding why the answer is not small requires first understanding the baseline response that every feedback modifies.

A warmer body radiates more. Differentiating the Stefan–Boltzmann law gives a change in emitted flux of four times sigma times temperature cubed, per kelvin of warming. At an effective emission temperature of 255 kelvin this evaluates to about 3.8 watts per square metre per kelvin. In climate work the convention is to write feedbacks as negative when they oppose the initial change, so this baseline is written as a Planck feedback parameter of roughly minus 3.2 watts per square metre per kelvin. The figure is a little smaller in magnitude than the naive 3.8 because the real atmosphere does not warm uniformly and because emission comes from a range of altitudes and spectral regions rather than a single blackbody surface.

The Planck response is the thermostat. It is what guarantees the climate system is stable at all: warm the planet and it radiates away the excess, cool it and it retains more. Without it, any perturbation would run away. With it alone, the equilibrium warming from a doubling of carbon dioxide would be the forcing divided by the feedback magnitude, about 3.9 divided by 3.2, or roughly 1.2 degrees Celsius. That figure, sometimes called the no-feedback or blackbody sensitivity, is the anchor against which everything else is measured, and it is not seriously disputed by anyone. It follows from spectroscopy and thermodynamics that were settled by 1900.

The whole scientific argument about sensitivity is therefore an argument about the factor by which feedbacks amplify that 1.2 degrees. Observed and modelled estimates of about 3 degrees imply an amplification factor near 2.5 to 3.

The standard formalism makes this precise. Write the top-of-atmosphere energy imbalance N as the forcing F plus lambda times the temperature change, where lambda is the total feedback parameter, negative for a stable system. At equilibrium the imbalance is zero, so the equilibrium temperature change equals minus F divided by lambda. Lambda is the sum of the Planck term and each additional feedback: water vapour, lapse rate, surface albedo, clouds, and smaller terms. If the sum of the non-Planck feedbacks is positive and approaches 3.2 in magnitude, lambda approaches zero and sensitivity diverges. This is the mathematical origin of the notorious asymmetry in the sensitivity distribution: because sensitivity depends on the reciprocal of a quantity that is itself uncertain, a symmetric uncertainty in lambda produces a strongly skewed distribution in sensitivity with a long tail toward high values. Halving lambda doubles the temperature; halving the temperature merely doubles lambda. That asymmetry is not a rhetorical trick or an artefact of pessimism. It is a property of division.

sections.heading: Water Vapour and the Lapse Rate
sections.body:
The largest amplifying feedback in the climate system is water vapour, and it is also the best understood, resting on a nineteenth-century equation and a straightforward physical argument.

Warm air can hold more water vapour. The Clausius–Clapeyron relation, derived from thermodynamics, gives the saturation vapour pressure of water as a function of temperature, and near typical surface temperatures it implies an increase of about 7 per cent per kelvin of warming. If relative humidity stays roughly constant — which is what happens when evaporation and precipitation both scale up together, and what both models and observations show to a good approximation — then the absolute amount of water vapour in the atmosphere rises by about 7 per cent per degree. Water vapour is itself a powerful greenhouse gas, so this constitutes a positive feedback: warming produces more vapour, which produces more warming.

The magnitude, computed from radiative transfer given the humidity change, is a feedback parameter of about plus 1.8 watts per square metre per kelvin, with the water vapour feedback alone roughly doubling the no-feedback sensitivity. Satellite measurements of upper-tropospheric humidity from instruments including the Atmospheric Infrared Sounder, and the observed response of atmospheric moisture to the eruption of Pinatubo and to El Niño events, confirm the expected scaling within their error bars. This is one of the few feedbacks that can be considered well constrained by direct observation.

Water vapour is often described as a feedback rather than a forcing, and the distinction is worth being exact about. Vapour has an atmospheric residence time of about nine days; the atmosphere cannot hold more of it than the temperature permits, and any excess rains out within days. Its concentration is therefore set by temperature rather than setting it. Carbon dioxide, with an effective residence measured in centuries, behaves as an external control knob. Both matter; only one can be turned by human hands.

Partly offsetting the water vapour feedback is the lapse rate feedback, and the two are so tightly coupled that they are usually assessed together. The lapse rate is the rate at which temperature falls with altitude. In the tropics, that rate is set by moist convection: rising air cools, condensation releases latent heat, and the resulting profile follows a moist adiabat. In a warmer, moister world, more latent heat is released aloft, so the upper troposphere warms more than the surface — the predicted tropical upper-tropospheric hot spot. A warmer upper troposphere radiates more efficiently to space, which is a negative feedback of about minus 0.5 to minus 0.6 watts per square metre per kelvin in the global mean.

Because both feedbacks derive from the same moist thermodynamics, models that produce a strong water vapour feedback also produce a strong lapse rate offset, and the combined value is better constrained than either alone: roughly plus 1.15 watts per square metre per kelvin, with high confidence.

sections.heading: Surface Albedo and the Cryosphere
sections.body:
Snow and sea ice reflect between 50 and 90 per cent of incident sunlight; open ocean reflects around 6 per cent and bare land typically 10 to 25 per cent. Melt the bright surface and the darker one beneath absorbs far more energy. This ice–albedo feedback is the most intuitive of all climate feedbacks and, in the polar regions, one of the most dramatic.

Its global magnitude is smaller than intuition suggests, at about plus 0.3 to plus 0.4 watts per square metre per kelvin, roughly a fifth of the water vapour feedback. Two factors limit it. First, the ice is at high latitudes where incident sunlight is weak and arrives at a grazing angle, so a square metre of newly exposed Arctic ocean absorbs much less than a square metre of newly exposed tropical ocean would. Second, polar regions receive no sunlight at all for months, and the greatest ice loss occurs in late summer as the Sun is already declining. Third, and often overlooked, low clouds are common over the Arctic ocean and partly mask the underlying surface from the perspective of space.

The regional effect, however, is anything but small. The Arctic has warmed at roughly three to four times the global average rate, a phenomenon called Arctic amplification, of which the albedo feedback is one contributor alongside changes in the vertical structure of warming, in cloud cover, in ocean heat transport, and in the way a stably stratified polar atmosphere confines warming near the surface. September Arctic sea ice extent has declined by roughly 13 per cent per decade since satellite records began in 1979, and multiyear thick ice has been largely replaced by thinner seasonal ice.

Land snow cover contributes a further component, concentrated in spring across Eurasia and North America, and the shortening of the snow season has itself been substantial. Ice sheets contribute over longer timescales: the Greenland and Antarctic sheets are large, bright and slow, and their surface albedo also darkens through the accumulation of dust, soot and pigmented algae in melt zones.

A frequently asked question is whether the ice–albedo feedback can run away. It can, and it has. The snowball Earth episodes of the Neoproterozoic, roughly 720 and 640 million years ago, are usually explained by exactly this instability: once ice advances past about 30 degrees latitude, where a large area receives strong sunlight, the feedback outpaces the Planck restoring force and glaciation runs to the equator. Escaping such a state requires volcanic carbon dioxide to accumulate for millions of years until the greenhouse forcing overwhelms the albedo. That instability is not a live concern today, because the modern Earth has far too little ice at low latitudes for the runaway to engage, and because the Sun is now roughly 6 per cent brighter than it was then.

sections.heading: Clouds: The Dominant Uncertainty
sections.body:
Clouds are where the sensitivity problem actually lives. They cover roughly two-thirds of the planet at any moment, and they influence the energy budget in two large and opposing ways. They reflect sunlight, cooling the surface, and they absorb and re-emit infrared radiation, warming it. In the present climate the cooling effect wins: clouds reduce absorbed solar radiation by about 47 watts per square metre and reduce outgoing infrared by about 27, for a net cooling of roughly 20 watts per square metre. Change that net figure by a small percentage and you change the planet's energy balance by as much as a doubling of carbon dioxide.

Which effect dominates depends overwhelmingly on cloud altitude, and secondarily on thickness and droplet size. Low clouds — marine stratocumulus decks off the west coasts of continents, trade cumulus over the subtropical oceans — have tops only a kilometre or two up, at nearly the same temperature as the surface beneath, so they emit nearly as much infrared as the surface would. They barely affect outgoing longwave radiation but reflect a great deal of sunlight, so they cool strongly. High clouds — cirrus, the anvils of deep convection — are thin, transmit much of the sunlight, and have tops at minus 50 degrees or colder, so they emit very little to space. They warm strongly.

The feedbacks follow. If warming reduces the coverage or brightness of subtropical low clouds, less sunlight is reflected and the planet warms further: a strong positive feedback. If high cloud tops rise so as to remain at roughly the same temperature — the fixed anvil temperature hypothesis, well supported theoretically and observationally — then they do not radiate more as the planet warms, and that too is positive. If deep convective anvils shrink in area as convection becomes more efficient in a warmer atmosphere, the iris hypothesis proposed by Richard Lindzen in 2001, that would be a negative feedback; the evidence for a strong iris effect is weak, though a modest version may operate.

The best current assessment puts the net cloud feedback at about plus 0.42 watts per square metre per kelvin, with a range from roughly minus 0.1 to plus 0.94. It is very likely positive — a conclusion that firmed up considerably in the 2010s through combined evidence from satellite observations of natural variability, from high-resolution simulations of individual cloud fields, and from process understanding of what controls stratocumulus decks. But its range remains wider than every other feedback combined and is the direct reason the sensitivity range remains wide.

The root difficulty is one of scale. Individual clouds are hundreds of metres across; global climate models have grid boxes tens to a hundred kilometres wide. Clouds must therefore be parameterised — represented by empirical rules relating grid-scale conditions to cloud amount — and different reasonable parameterisations give different feedbacks. Kilometre-scale global models now being built are the most promising route past this bottleneck.

sections.heading: Three Different Sensitivities, Often Confused
sections.body:
The word sensitivity is used for at least three distinct quantities with different values and different uses, and conflating them is the most common error in public discussion of the subject.

Equilibrium climate sensitivity is the warming after the system has fully adjusted to a doubled carbon dioxide concentration, holding the ice sheets, vegetation and the carbon cycle fixed at present-day states. Only the fast components — atmosphere, ocean, sea ice, snow, clouds — are allowed to respond. This is the Charney sensitivity, best estimated at 3 degrees Celsius. Full equilibration takes one to two thousand years because the deep ocean takes that long to warm, so this number is not directly observable; it must be inferred.

Transient climate response is the warming at the moment carbon dioxide reaches double its initial value, in an idealised experiment where concentration rises at 1 per cent per year, taking about seventy years. It is smaller than equilibrium sensitivity because the ocean is still absorbing heat and the system has not caught up. Best estimate 1.8 degrees, likely range 1.4 to 2.2. This is the more policy-relevant figure for the coming century, and importantly it is better constrained than equilibrium sensitivity because it depends less on the poorly known long-tail behaviour and more on quantities we can observe now.

Earth system sensitivity includes the slow feedbacks: growth or collapse of ice sheets, migration of vegetation zones, and the release of carbon from soils, permafrost and the ocean. It applies on timescales of millennia and is substantially larger, plausibly 1.5 to 2 times the equilibrium value, though estimates are loose. Paleoclimate reconstructions that compare deep-time carbon dioxide with deep-time temperature are measuring something closer to this quantity than to Charney sensitivity, and correcting for that difference is a large part of the technical work in paleo estimates.

A fourth quantity has become increasingly important for policy: the transient climate response to cumulative emissions, or TCRE, defined as the warming per trillion tonnes of carbon emitted. Observations and models agree it is close to constant, at about 1.65 degrees per trillion tonnes of carbon, with a likely range of 1.0 to 2.3. Its near-constancy arises because the diminishing radiative return from each additional tonne, from the logarithmic law, is offset by the diminishing efficiency of ocean and land carbon uptake as those reservoirs fill. That coincidence is what makes the idea of a fixed carbon budget coherent: warming depends on the total amount emitted rather than on the path.

A fifth term appears in modern literature: effective climate sensitivity, the value inferred by extrapolating from a period of a few decades using the energy balance relation, as distinct from the true equilibrium value that would be reached eventually. The two differ, generally with the effective value lower, for reasons connected to the changing geographic pattern of warming.

sections.heading: Estimating Sensitivity from the Instrumental Record
sections.body:
The most direct-seeming approach is to use the warming already observed. The energy balance method rearranges the basic relation: sensitivity equals the forcing for a doubling, multiplied by the observed temperature change, divided by the difference between the total forcing and the current planetary energy imbalance. Everything on the right-hand side is in principle measurable.

Each term brings its own difficulty. Global mean surface temperature change since the 1850–1900 baseline is about 1.1 to 1.2 degrees, known to roughly a tenth of a degree, and is the best-constrained input, though there are genuine subtleties about how sea surface temperature measurements from buckets, engine intakes, drifting buoys and satellites are stitched together, and about whether sparse early coverage of the Arctic biases the trend low. Total anthropogenic forcing is about 2.7 watts per square metre but with a large uncertainty dominated entirely by aerosols. The planetary energy imbalance — the rate at which the Earth is currently accumulating heat, over 90 per cent of it in the ocean — is now measured with genuine precision at roughly 0.7 to 0.9 watts per square metre, thanks to the Argo array of nearly 4,000 autonomous profiling floats deployed from 2000 onward, which measure temperature and salinity to 2,000 metres depth, and to the CERES satellite instruments that track the top-of-atmosphere flux change accurately even though their absolute calibration is not sufficient for a standalone measurement.

Plug in central values and the arithmetic gives something near 3.9 times 1.15 divided by 1.9, or about 2.4 degrees. Studies of this kind published between 2012 and 2015, notably by Nicholas Lewis and Judith Curry, produced central estimates around 1.6 to 2.0 degrees for equilibrium sensitivity and were widely cited as evidence that mainstream estimates were too high.

Three subsequent findings substantially rehabilitated the higher values. First, the pattern effect: warming so far has been concentrated in places, particularly the western tropical Pacific and the Southern Ocean, whose feedbacks differ from those of the regions expected to warm later, making the recent record misleadingly reassuring. Second, the historical record blends a strongly negative aerosol forcing with the greenhouse forcing, and if aerosol cooling is at the weaker end of its range then the inferred sensitivity rises steeply; the method is acutely sensitive to a badly constrained quantity. Third, the method estimates effective rather than equilibrium sensitivity, and the gap between them is estimated at several tens of per cent.

The honest summary is that the historical record on its own constrains sensitivity only loosely, rules out very high values less well than one would hope, and rules out very low values quite firmly — a sensitivity below about 1.5 degrees cannot reproduce the observed warming given any plausible aerosol forcing.

sections.heading: Evidence from the Deep Past
sections.body:
Paleoclimate offers something the instrumental record cannot: large forcings, fully equilibrated responses, and states of the climate system quite different from today's. Its cost is that everything must be reconstructed from proxies with their own uncertainties.

The best-studied interval is the Last Glacial Maximum, about 20,000 years ago. Carbon dioxide, measured directly in air bubbles trapped in Antarctic ice cores, stood at about 190 parts per million against a pre-industrial 280. Vast ice sheets covered North America and northern Europe, sea level was roughly 120 metres lower, and dust loading was far higher. Reconstructed global mean temperature was about 5 to 6 degrees colder than pre-industrial, a figure firmed up considerably by data assimilation studies published around 2020 that combined marine and terrestrial proxies with model physics. Dividing the temperature change by the total forcing, including the ice sheets and dust as forcings rather than feedbacks, yields an equilibrium sensitivity in the range of roughly 2 to 4.5 degrees.

Deeper time provides other anchors. The Pliocene warm period around 3 million years ago had carbon dioxide near 400 parts per million, similar to today, and global temperatures 2.5 to 4 degrees warmer with sea level perhaps 20 metres higher — a picture of what the slower Earth system sensitivity implies for a world that stays at present concentrations. The Paleocene–Eocene Thermal Maximum 56 million years ago saw a rapid carbon release, probably several thousand billion tonnes over a few thousand years, accompanied by 5 to 6 degrees of warming and severe ocean acidification, giving sensitivity estimates broadly consistent with 3 degrees but with wide error bars on the carbon release. The Cretaceous and early Eocene hothouses show polar regions far warmer than models easily reproduce, hinting that sensitivity may increase in warmer states.

Two systematic difficulties limit paleo estimates. The first is that they measure Earth system sensitivity, including ice sheet and vegetation responses, so converting them to Charney sensitivity requires reclassifying some responses as forcings, which is a modelling judgement rather than a measurement. The second is the state dependence problem: the Last Glacial Maximum was a cold world with extensive ice, and the feedbacks operating there, particularly the ice–albedo feedback, are not the same ones that will operate in a warm world with little ice. There is reasonable evidence that sensitivity is somewhat higher in warmer states, meaning glacial estimates may understate the value relevant to the coming centuries.

Deep time adds a third complication. Solar luminosity rises by roughly 7 per cent per billion years, and continental positions, ocean gateways and mountain ranges all differed, altering heat transport and the pattern of warming. Careful studies correct for these, but the residual uncertainty grows with age, which is why the Last Glacial Maximum and the Pliocene carry more weight than the Cretaceous despite the latter's larger signal.

Taken together, paleoclimate independently supports a value near 3 degrees, excludes values below about 1.5 quite strongly, and does relatively little to exclude values above 4.5.

sections.heading: Models, Emergent Constraints and the 2020 Synthesis
sections.body:
General circulation models solve the equations of fluid motion, thermodynamics and radiative transfer on a three-dimensional grid covering the atmosphere and ocean. Their sensitivity is not programmed in; it emerges from the interaction of the represented physics, and can only be discovered by running the model and measuring the result. Historically the spread across models has been wide, and it has never narrowed much: the models participating in the fifth Coupled Model Intercomparison Project, used for the 2013 assessment, spanned about 2.1 to 4.7 degrees.

The sixth generation, CMIP6, produced a genuine surprise. Several prominent models came out with sensitivities above 5 degrees, some approaching 5.6, and the multi-model range widened to roughly 1.8 to 5.6 degrees. Investigation traced this almost entirely to revised treatments of cloud microphysics, specifically the mixed-phase cloud feedback: older models converted supercooled liquid to ice too readily, and correcting this to match observations left more liquid in high-latitude clouds, which then had more scope to be depleted by warming, producing a stronger positive feedback. Whether the new treatment is right remains contested, and the hot models notably fail to reproduce the observed temperature record of the twentieth century, warming too much.

The response of the assessment community was decisive and represents a methodological shift worth understanding. The 2020 World Climate Research Programme assessment led by Steven Sherwood and colleagues, and the IPCC report that followed, declined to derive sensitivity from the model spread at all. Instead they combined three independent lines of evidence in a Bayesian framework: process understanding of individual feedbacks, the historical instrumental record, and paleoclimate. Because the three lines have largely independent errors, their combination is far sharper than any alone. The result narrowed the likely range for the first time in forty years, from the Charney era's 1.5 to 4.5 down to 2.5 to 4, with a very likely range of 2 to 5. Models were then handled by weighting or screening: projections in the 2021 report used model-democracy-free assessed ranges rather than raw multi-model means.

Emergent constraints are a related technique. The idea is to find an observable feature of the present climate — the strength of tropical low cloud variability, the seasonal cycle of albedo, the degree of mixing between the boundary layer and the free troposphere — that correlates across models with their sensitivity, then use the observed value of that feature to select which models to believe. Dozens have been proposed. In practice they disagree with each other, many correlations weaken as more models are added, and the danger of finding a spurious relationship among many candidates is real. They are best treated as one contributing strand rather than a decisive method, which is broadly how the 2020 assessment treated them.

sections.heading: The Pattern Effect and Why Sensitivity Is Not Constant
sections.body:
One of the most important developments of the past decade is the realisation that the feedback parameter is not a single fixed number even for a given planet. It depends on where the warming happens, and the geographic pattern of warming changes over time. This is called the pattern effect, and it reconciles what had looked like a genuine conflict between historical and model-based estimates.

The mechanism runs through the tropical atmosphere. Deep convection in the warmest parts of the tropical ocean, chiefly the western Pacific warm pool, sets the temperature profile of the entire tropical free troposphere, because the tropics cannot sustain large horizontal temperature gradients aloft. Warming concentrated in those convecting regions therefore warms the free troposphere everywhere in the tropics. That warmer air aloft, sitting above the cool eastern Pacific and the subtropical stratocumulus decks, strengthens the temperature inversion that caps the boundary layer, which stabilises and thickens the low cloud decks. More low cloud means more reflected sunlight and a strongly negative feedback. Conversely, warming concentrated in the eastern Pacific or the subtropics weakens the inversion, breaks up the low cloud, and produces a positive feedback.

Over the historical period the observed warming pattern has been unusual: the eastern equatorial Pacific has warmed slowly or not at all, while the western Pacific warm pool has warmed substantially, and the Southern Ocean has warmed very little. That pattern is the low-sensitivity one. It has made the recent decades appear more stable than the long-run equilibrium, and it is the leading explanation for why energy-balance estimates from the instrumental record came out low. Models forced with observed sea surface temperature patterns reproduce the low apparent feedback; the same models run freely produce a different pattern and a higher one.

The unresolved question, and it is genuinely unresolved, is whether the observed pattern is internal variability that will reverse, or a forced response that will persist. If it is variability, the historical record understates sensitivity and the pattern will eventually shift toward the model behaviour, with a corresponding acceleration of warming. If the models are systematically wrong about the tropical Pacific — and there is a known model bias, the double intertropical convergence zone problem, that suggests they might be — then the low apparent sensitivity may be closer to real. The literature since about 2018 leans toward the first interpretation, partly because the observed trend is at the very edge of what model internal variability produces, but the matter is contested and honest researchers disagree.

Beyond the pattern effect, sensitivity is also state dependent: feedbacks in a colder icier world differ from those in a warm ice-free one, and there is evidence for a modest increase in sensitivity with temperature. The practical implication is that sensitivity should be thought of as a locally applicable slope rather than a universal constant.

sections.heading: Failure Modes, Limits and What the Uncertainty Means
sections.body:
Several recurring errors follow from misunderstanding what these quantities are, and it is worth naming them plainly.

The first is treating sensitivity as a prediction. It is not. It is a property of the system, an exchange rate between forcing and temperature. What actually happens depends on emissions, which are a matter of human choice, and on the timescale considered. Quoting a sensitivity of 3 degrees does not mean the world will warm 3 degrees; it means that if concentrations double and stay doubled, it eventually will.

The second is conflating the three sensitivities. Someone citing 1.8 degrees and someone citing 3 degrees may agree completely, one quoting transient response and the other equilibrium. Similarly, paleoclimate estimates that seem alarmingly high are often Earth system sensitivity, which properly includes ice sheet loss over millennia.

The third is the saturation argument — that carbon dioxide's absorption bands are already full, so more cannot matter. The band centre is saturated; the wings are not, and the logarithmic law is precisely the mathematical expression of partial saturation. Each doubling still adds about 3.9 watts per square metre, and there is no concentration at which this stops.

The fourth is treating the uncertainty range as symmetric evidence for optimism. Because equilibrium warming is the forcing divided by a feedback parameter that could be near zero, the probability distribution has a long right tail. A range of 2 to 5 degrees is not a coin flip around 3.5; the tail beyond 5 carries small probability but very large consequences, and any sensible treatment of risk weights it accordingly. Symmetrically, low values below 1.5 are excluded by multiple independent lines of evidence, so the range is genuinely bounded below.

The fifth error concerns tipping points. Sensitivity as conventionally defined assumes a smooth, roughly linear response. Several components of the Earth system — the West Antarctic and Greenland ice sheets, the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation, permafrost carbon, tropical forest dieback — may have thresholds beyond which change becomes self-sustaining. These sit largely outside the sensitivity framework, which is a statement about its limits rather than a criticism of it.

What to do with all this in practice is unglamorous but clear. Use transient response, or better the cumulative-emissions relationship, for questions about this century; use equilibrium sensitivity for questions about eventual outcomes; use Earth system sensitivity for questions about sea level over millennia. Treat the assessed ranges rather than any single model. Recognise that the largest remaining scientific uncertainty is the behaviour of low clouds in the subtropics, that the largest remaining forcing uncertainty is aerosols, and that both are actively being narrowed by kilometre-scale modelling and by satellite records that lengthen every year. And recognise that the uncertainty, whatever its eventual resolution, has never been large enough to make the problem go away.

guides.title: Paleoclimatology — Reading Past Climates
guides.summary: How scientists reconstruct the Earth's climate before thermometers existed, using ice cores, ocean sediments, tree rings, cave deposits and corals. Covers the physics of each proxy, how records are dated, what the deep past reveals, and where reconstructions go wrong.

sections.heading: Why the Climate of the Past Is Worth Knowing
sections.body:
Direct measurement of the Earth's temperature with instruments began in earnest around 1850, and even then only across a scattering of European and North American stations, a handful of colonial outposts, and the decks of merchant ships that measured seawater by hauling up a canvas bucket. That gives roughly 175 years of numbers. The Earth's climate system, by contrast, has been running for about 4.5 billion years, and the parts of it that matter for understanding the present — the growth and collapse of ice sheets, the reorganisation of ocean currents, the response of the carbon cycle to warming — operate on timescales of centuries to hundreds of thousands of years. Trying to understand climate from the instrumental record alone is like trying to characterise a symphony from four seconds of tape.

Paleoclimatology is the discipline that extends the record backwards. It does so indirectly, by finding natural materials whose physical or chemical properties were set by the climate at the moment they formed, and which then survived without further alteration. A layer of snow that fell on Antarctica 400,000 years ago carries in the ratio of its oxygen isotopes a signature of the temperature at which the water vapour condensed. A bubble of air sealed into that same layer as it compacted into ice is a literal sample of the ancient atmosphere, containing the carbon dioxide and methane that were present. A shell secreted by a microscopic marine organism records both the temperature and the chemistry of the seawater it grew in. These are called proxies: stand-ins for a measurement nobody was there to make.

The stakes are practical, not merely antiquarian. Three questions in particular depend on the paleo record. First, how sensitive is the climate to a given change in greenhouse gases? The instrumental record covers only a narrow range of forcing, so the constraint on climate sensitivity — usually expressed as the warming from doubling carbon dioxide, currently estimated at roughly 2.5 to 4 degrees Celsius with the tails poorly constrained — leans heavily on past warm and cold states. Second, how fast can the system change? The paleo record contains abrupt transitions, some of them regional warmings of 10 degrees or more within a human lifetime, which no observation of the modern era would have suggested were possible. Third, what is normal? Judging whether a modern trend is unusual requires knowing the range of natural variability, and that range only becomes visible over millennia.

There is also a humbling lesson embedded in the enterprise. Every proxy is a compromise. None of them measures temperature; all of them measure something correlated with temperature, entangled with other influences that must be disentangled by argument and calibration. The confidence one can place in a reconstruction is a function of how many independent proxies agree, how well each is understood physically, and how honestly the practitioners report what they do not know.

sections.heading: The Central Problem: Proxies Are Not Thermometers
sections.body:
A thermometer has a single, well-characterised relationship to the quantity it measures. Mercury expands with temperature according to a known coefficient; the reading is a direct function of one variable. No natural climate archive works this way. Every proxy responds to several environmental influences at once, and the task of the paleoclimatologist is to isolate the climate signal from everything else that shaped the material.

Consider tree rings, the most intuitive proxy. A tree in a cold, high-latitude forest grows a wide ring in a warm summer and a narrow one in a cold summer, because temperature is the factor limiting its growth. The same species growing at the arid lower edge of its range produces wide rings in wet years and narrow ones in dry years, because water, not warmth, is the constraint. The width of a ring is therefore not a temperature measurement; it is a measurement of whatever was scarcest. Choosing sampling sites where a single variable dominates — the principle of the limiting factor, articulated by the astronomer A. E. Douglass in the early twentieth century when he founded the field — is the first and most consequential decision in any reconstruction.

The same ambiguity runs through every archive. The oxygen isotope ratio in a marine carbonate shell depends on both the temperature of the water and the isotopic composition of the water itself, which in turn depends on how much of the planet's light isotopes are locked up in continental ice. A single measurement cannot separate the two; the separation requires either an independent temperature proxy or an assumption about ice volume. The ratio of magnesium to calcium in that same shell responds mainly to temperature but is also sensitive to seawater pH and to dissolution on the sea floor after death. Pollen counts in a lake sediment reflect the surrounding vegetation, but vegetation responds to temperature, precipitation, soil, fire history, and the simple lag of how long it takes forests to migrate.

Three strategies address this. The first is multi-proxy work: combining archives whose confounding factors differ, on the reasoning that if independent methods with independent biases agree, the shared signal is more likely real. The second is calibration, in which the proxy is measured over the instrumental period and regressed against actual observations, producing a transfer function that is then extrapolated backwards. This is powerful but carries an unavoidable assumption of stationarity — that the relationship holding during the calibration window also held in the past, which cannot be tested directly. The third is mechanistic modelling, in which the physics or biology of the proxy is simulated forward from a climate state, so that a reconstruction becomes a matter of finding the climate that best explains the observed proxy rather than inverting a statistical fit.

None of these removes uncertainty. Honest reconstructions publish error bars, and those error bars often widen dramatically as one goes further back, because both the density of records and the quality of the dating deteriorate. A reconstruction quoted without an uncertainty range should be treated with suspicion.

sections.heading: Stable Isotopes: The Master Key
sections.body:
More paleoclimate information comes from stable isotope ratios than from any other single measurement, so it is worth understanding the physics properly rather than treating it as a black box. Oxygen occurs in nature as three stable isotopes: oxygen-16, which makes up about 99.76 percent of the total, oxygen-18 at about 0.20 percent, and oxygen-17 at a trace. Hydrogen occurs as ordinary hydrogen and as deuterium, roughly one atom in 6,400. Molecules built from the heavier isotopes are chemically almost identical but physically slightly different: they are marginally heavier, they vibrate at lower frequencies, and they are therefore very slightly more strongly bound and less volatile.

That small difference has large consequences during phase changes. When seawater evaporates, molecules containing oxygen-16 escape preferentially, because they require slightly less energy to leave the liquid. The resulting water vapour is depleted in oxygen-18 relative to the ocean. When that vapour later condenses into rain or snow, the reverse happens: the heavier molecules condense preferentially, so the first rain to fall from an air mass is relatively enriched in oxygen-18 and the remaining vapour becomes progressively more depleted. This progressive stripping is called Rayleigh distillation, and it means that the isotopic composition of precipitation depends on how much condensation has already occurred along the air mass's path — which depends in turn on temperature, distance from the moisture source, and altitude.

Results are reported not as raw ratios but as delta values in parts per thousand, written with the per mil symbol. The definition is straightforward: delta oxygen-18 equals the sample's heavy-to-light ratio divided by a standard's ratio, minus one, times 1,000. The standard for water is Vienna Standard Mean Ocean Water; for carbonates it is usually Vienna Pee Dee Belemnite. A value of minus 40 per mil, typical of central Antarctic snow, means the sample contains 4 percent less oxygen-18 than mean ocean water.

Empirically, in the mid and high latitudes, the delta oxygen-18 of precipitation rises by roughly 0.6 to 0.7 per mil for every degree Celsius of warming at the condensation site, a relationship first mapped systematically by Willi Dansgaard in 1964. Deuterium follows a parallel relationship about eight times as steep. This is the basis of ice core thermometry. The catch is that the slope is not constant through time: changes in the seasonality of snowfall, in the moisture source region, or in the elevation of the ice surface all shift it, and corrections derived from borehole temperature profiles suggest the glacial-age slope in Greenland was roughly half the modern spatial slope, which nearly doubled the estimated ice age cooling there.

In marine carbonates the same isotope system works differently. A shell precipitated in equilibrium with seawater is enriched in oxygen-18 relative to the water by an amount that decreases as temperature rises, at about 0.2 per mil per degree. Because global ice volume also shifts ocean delta oxygen-18 by about 1 per mil between glacial and interglacial extremes, the marine signal is a mixture of temperature and ice volume that must be untangled.

sections.heading: Ice Cores: Layered Snow and Trapped Air
sections.body:
An ice core is the closest thing paleoclimatology has to a direct measurement, because it preserves two independent kinds of information in the same column: the isotopic composition of the snow, which encodes temperature, and actual bubbles of ancient air, which encode atmospheric composition. Nothing else in the natural world stores a physical sample of the past atmosphere.

The mechanism is simple accumulation. Snow falls on an ice sheet, is buried by later snow, and compacts under load. In the upper 50 to 120 metres, called the firn, the snowpack remains permeable and air circulates freely through the pore space. Below a critical density of about 830 kilograms per cubic metre the pores pinch off and the air is sealed into discrete bubbles. This produces a crucial and often misunderstood consequence: the air in a bubble is always younger than the ice enclosing it, because it kept exchanging with the atmosphere while the ice around it was already decades or centuries old. At the high-accumulation Greenland sites this gas-age–ice-age difference is a few decades; at the cold, dry, slow-accumulating East Antarctic domes it can exceed 5,000 years. Correcting for it is essential when comparing a gas record to a temperature record from the same core, and errors here have caused genuine controversies over whether carbon dioxide led or lagged temperature at glacial terminations.

Deeper still, below roughly 500 to 1,200 metres, the bubbles collapse entirely as air molecules are forced into the crystal lattice, forming clathrate hydrates. The gas is still there and still measurable, but extracting it requires crushing or melting rather than simple mechanical release, and the transition zone produces analytical artefacts that must be handled with care.

The major drilling projects define the field's reach. The Greenland cores GRIP, GISP2 and NGRIP reach back roughly 123,000 years with annual layer resolution over much of that span, because Greenland accumulation is high enough that individual years remain distinguishable by dust, chemistry and isotopes. In Antarctica the Vostok core reached about 420,000 years, and the EPICA Dome C core extended the composite record to about 800,000 years, covering eight full glacial cycles. Older ice exists in patches: so-called blue ice areas where old ice is exposed by ablation have yielded samples over a million years old, and the Beyond EPICA project has been drilling for a continuous 1.5-million-year record specifically to investigate why the glacial rhythm shifted from 41,000 to 100,000 years around a million years ago.

Beyond isotopes and gases, an ice core carries a rich secondary archive. Sulphate spikes date volcanic eruptions and provide tie points between cores in both hemispheres. Dust concentration indexes continental aridity and wind strength; glacial-age Antarctic ice can carry 20 to 50 times the dust of interglacial ice. Sea salt indexes storminess and sea ice extent. Beryllium-10, produced by cosmic rays, tracks solar activity and geomagnetic field strength. Ammonium and levoglucosan record biomass burning. A single metre of ice can be analysed a dozen different ways.

sections.heading: Ocean Sediment Cores and the Foraminifera
sections.body:
The deep sea floor accumulates a slow, continuous rain of material — the shells of dead plankton, wind-blown dust, volcanic ash, clay — at rates typically between one and ten centimetres per thousand years. Because the abyss is cold, dark, and largely undisturbed, this accumulation builds an orderly stack that can be sampled by pushing or drilling a tube into the sea bed. Ocean sediment cores are the backbone of long-timescale paleoclimatology: they extend continuously over tens of millions of years, they are globally distributed, and they carry a dozen distinct proxy systems in a single sample.

The workhorse organism is the foraminifer, a single-celled protist that builds a chambered shell of calcium carbonate. Planktonic species live in the upper water column and record surface conditions; benthic species live on or in the sea floor and record deep water properties. Because deep water temperature varies little, benthic oxygen isotope records are dominated by global ice volume, which makes them the standard yardstick of glacial cycles. The stacked benthic record assembled by Lorraine Lisiecki and Maureen Raymo in 2005 from 57 globally distributed cores, universally known as LR04, is the reference chronology against which almost every other Pleistocene record is aligned.

Several independent measurements can be made on the same shells. Oxygen isotopes give the temperature-plus-ice-volume signal. The ratio of magnesium to calcium substituted into the carbonate lattice increases with temperature by roughly 9 percent per degree Celsius, giving an independent thermometer that, combined with oxygen isotopes on the same shell, allows ice volume to be solved for. Carbon isotopes in benthic shells trace the ventilation and nutrient content of deep water masses, distinguishing for instance North Atlantic Deep Water from Antarctic Bottom Water. Boron isotopes and the boron-to-calcium ratio respond to seawater pH and therefore to dissolved carbon dioxide, offering one of the few ways to estimate atmospheric carbon dioxide before ice cores exist. The species assemblage itself is informative, since different foraminifera prefer different temperature ranges.

Organic molecules add further channels. Alkenones, long-chain compounds produced by certain coccolithophore algae, contain a number of double bonds that varies systematically with growth temperature; the index built from them, written UK'37, calibrates to sea surface temperature with an accuracy of about 1.5 degrees. Membrane lipids from archaea give the independent TEX86 thermometer, useful in warm settings where alkenones saturate.

The limitations are real. Burrowing animals mix the top 5 to 10 centimetres of sediment, smearing the record and setting a resolution floor of a few centuries at typical accumulation rates. Below the carbonate compensation depth, roughly 4,000 to 5,000 metres depending on ocean basin, calcium carbonate dissolves and the foraminiferal record simply disappears. Slumps, turbidity currents and current-driven erosion can remove or duplicate sections. And the sea floor older than about 180 million years has almost entirely been subducted, which is why the marine record of deeper time relies on uplifted marine rocks exposed on land.

sections.heading: Tree Rings and the Discipline of Dendroclimatology
sections.body:
In temperate and boreal climates a tree adds one growth increment per year, producing large thin-walled cells in spring and smaller thick-walled ones later in the season, so that each year appears as a visible band. Counting inward from the bark gives an exactly dated calendar, and the width, density or chemistry of each ring records the conditions of that specific growing season. No other proxy delivers this combination of annual resolution and absolute, error-free dating.

The technique that makes it rigorous is crossdating, developed by A. E. Douglass around 1904 while he was investigating whether sunspot cycles left a trace in Arizona pines. Trees in a common climate share a common pattern of good and bad years, so the ring-width sequence from one tree can be matched against another like a barcode. Matching a living tree to a dead snag, the snag to a beam in an archaeological ruin, and that beam to still older timber builds a continuous chronology far beyond the lifespan of any single tree. The bristlecone pine chronology of the White Mountains of California runs continuously beyond 8,000 years; European oak and pine chronologies assembled from riverbed and bog timbers exceed 12,000 years and now bridge into the late glacial. Crossdating also catches the two failure modes of naive counting: a missing ring in a year so bad the tree grew nothing, and a false ring produced by a mid-season drought and recovery.

Turning ring widths into climate requires removing the tree's own biology. A young tree adds wood to a small circumference and so produces wide rings; the same volume of wood spread over an older, larger trunk produces a narrower ring. This age-related trend is stripped by fitting a curve — a negative exponential, a spline, or a regional curve — and dividing the measured widths by it, producing a dimensionless index centred on one. The choice of curve is consequential. Aggressive detrending with short splines removes low-frequency variability along with the biological trend, so a chronology detrended that way cannot resolve century-scale changes at all. This is the segment length curse: no standard detrending can recover variability on timescales longer than the individual tree segments. Regional curve standardisation and signal-free methods attempt to preserve it, at the cost of other assumptions.

Beyond width, maximum latewood density — measured by X-ray densitometry or, more recently, by blue reflectance of a sanded surface — correlates more tightly with summer temperature than width does and responds with less lag. Stable isotopes in cellulose add a moisture and humidity signal. Frost rings and light rings mark specific catastrophic seasons, and several have been tied to known volcanic eruptions, notably the frost damage of 1601 following the 1600 Huaynaputina eruption in Peru.

The limits are geographical and temporal. Trees do not grow on ice, in the open ocean, or in most deserts, and tropical trees often lack clear annual rings because there is no dormant season. The record also thins rapidly before about 1,000 years ago simply because fewer old wood samples survive.

sections.heading: Caves, Corals, Lakes and Pollen: The Continental and Tropical Archives
sections.body:
Ice and deep-sea mud dominate the long records, but they leave the tropics and the continental interiors thinly sampled. Four further archives fill those gaps, and between them supply most of what is known about past rainfall.

Speleothems are the mineral deposits that grow inside caves: stalagmites rising from the floor, flowstone sheeting down walls. Rainwater percolating through soil picks up carbon dioxide from roots and microbes, turns mildly acidic, and dissolves limestone on its way down. Reaching the cave void, the solution degasses and precipitates calcium carbonate in thin laminae that are sometimes annual. The oxygen isotope composition of those laminae tracks the composition of rainfall above the cave, which in the tropics is governed less by temperature than by the total amount of rainfall. That makes speleothems the premier archive of monsoon strength, and the Chinese cave records from Hulu, Dongge and Sanbao reconstruct East Asian monsoon intensity over the past 640,000 years. Their decisive advantage is chronological: uranium-thorium dating gives absolute ages to within a few years in the Holocene and a few hundred at 500,000, independent of layer counting, which makes speleothems the tie points anchoring other archives.

Corals lay down annual density bands visible in X-ray, and their aragonite skeletons record sea surface conditions at roughly monthly resolution through oxygen isotopes and through the ratio of strontium to calcium, which is a clean temperature proxy. Because corals live in the tropical surface ocean they capture El Niño variability directly, and fossil corals uplifted on tectonically rising coasts in Papua New Guinea and Vanuatu open windows onto El Niño behaviour tens of thousands of years ago. Coral terraces also fix past sea level, since a species with a known depth habitat, dated by uranium series and surveyed for elevation, marks where the ocean surface once stood.

Lake sediments are the continental counterpart of marine cores. Where a lake has strong seasonal productivity and anoxic bottom water that excludes burrowing animals, sediment accumulates as varves: paired light and dark laminae, one couplet per year, countable like tree rings. Varved sequences from Lake Suigetsu in Japan and Meerfelder Maar in Germany provide independently dated late glacial and Holocene chronologies. Lake cores also carry diatoms, charcoal that indexes fire frequency, and chironomid head capsules, whose species assemblages shift sharply with July air temperature and supply one of the few quantitative continental thermometers.

Pollen is the most widely used continental proxy of all. Its outer wall is made of sporopollenin, among the most chemically resistant organic materials known, so grains survive tens of thousands of years in lake mud and their sculptured surfaces identify the parent plant to genus. Counting several hundred grains per sample converts a core into a vegetation history, and because plant communities have known climatic tolerances the assemblage can be translated into quantitative estimates of July temperature and annual precipitation. Fossil beetles complement pollen well: their exoskeletons preserve intact, most species have tight thermal tolerances that have not measurably shifted in hundreds of thousands of years, and because beetles fly they track abrupt change within years rather than the centuries forests need to migrate.

sections.heading: Building a Chronology: Dating the Archive
sections.body:
A proxy measurement without an age is useless. Establishing when each sample formed is often harder than measuring the climate signal, and it is where most disagreements between records originate.

The strongest chronologies come from counting annual layers. Tree rings, varved lake sediments, banded corals and high-accumulation ice all deposit one identifiable increment per year, and where crossdating or independent replication confirms the count, the result is an absolute calendar age with essentially zero error. The Greenland ice core chronology GICC05 was built this way by counting layers in multiple parameters, and carries a maximum counting error of about 2 percent at 60,000 years — roughly 1,200 years — which is excellent for a record of that length but not negligible.

Radiocarbon dating covers the past roughly 55,000 years and is the workhorse for organic material. Cosmic rays produce carbon-14 in the upper atmosphere; living organisms take it up in equilibrium with the atmosphere; on death the intake stops and the isotope decays with a half-life of 5,730 years. The complication is that atmospheric carbon-14 production has not been constant, so a raw radiocarbon age must be calibrated against a curve built from independently dated material — tree rings back about 14,000 years, then varves, speleothems and corals beyond. The current curve, IntCal20, converts radiocarbon years to calendar years with uncertainties that are small in the Holocene but widen at plateaus where the curve flattens and a single radiocarbon age maps to several centuries. Marine samples additionally need a reservoir correction of typically 400 years, more in upwelling regions, because deep water carries old carbon.

Uranium-series dating is the most precise method for carbonates. Uranium is soluble and is incorporated into growing speleothems and corals; thorium is insoluble and is essentially absent at formation. Thorium-230 then accumulates from uranium-234 decay at a known rate, so the thorium-to-uranium ratio gives an age with no assumption about initial conditions. The method works to roughly 600,000 years with precision of 0.1 to 1 percent.

Beyond that, other clocks take over. Luminescence dating measures the trapped-electron dose accumulated in quartz or feldspar grains since they were last exposed to sunlight, useful for dunes and loess back to several hundred thousand years. Argon-argon dating of volcanic ash layers gives absolute tie points in deep time. Cosmogenic nuclides date exposed rock surfaces.

Where no absolute method applies, records are dated by tuning: assuming that a feature in the record corresponds to a known astronomical cycle or to a dated feature elsewhere, and stretching the time axis to fit. Orbital tuning of marine cores is standard practice and works well, but it embeds an assumption about phase relationships and therefore cannot be used to test the very orbital theory it assumes. This circularity is a genuine and acknowledged weakness. Volcanic ash layers and abrupt methane transitions provide independent synchronisation between ice cores and other archives.

sections.heading: Orbital Forcing and the Rhythm of the Ice Ages
sections.body:
The single greatest success of paleoclimatology is the demonstration that the ice ages march to an astronomical beat. The Earth's orbit and spin axis are not fixed; they are perturbed by the gravity of Jupiter, Saturn, the Moon and the other planets, and these perturbations redistribute sunlight across latitude and season in a quasi-periodic way.

Three parameters matter. Eccentricity describes how elliptical the orbit is; it varies between nearly circular and about 0.058 with dominant periods near 100,000 and 405,000 years. It changes the total annual sunlight the Earth receives by at most about 0.2 percent, which is far too little to drive an ice age directly, but it modulates the strength of the other two effects. Obliquity is the tilt of the spin axis, oscillating between about 22.1 and 24.5 degrees with a period of 41,000 years; higher tilt means stronger seasons in both hemispheres and, importantly, more summer sunlight at high latitudes. Precession is the wobble of the axis combined with the rotation of the orbit itself, which shifts which season occurs at the closest approach to the Sun, with periods near 19,000 and 23,000 years. Precession changes seasonal contrast in opposite senses in the two hemispheres.

Milutin Milanković, a Serbian engineer working through the 1920s and 1930s, computed the resulting summer insolation curves by hand and proposed that ice sheets grow when summer sunlight at around 65 degrees north is weak enough that the previous winter's snow survives the melt season. Winter cold is not the constraint — high latitudes are always cold enough to snow — the constraint is whether summer removes it. The hypothesis languished for decades until 1976, when James Hays, John Imbrie and Nicholas Shackleton analysed two Indian Ocean sediment cores and found spectral peaks at 100,000, 42,000 and 23,000 years, matching the orbital periods with the correct phases. Their paper, titled "Variations in the Earth's Orbit: Pacemaker of the Ice Ages", settled the matter.

Two genuine puzzles remain. The first is the 100,000-year problem. Over the past 800,000 years glacial cycles have had a dominant period near 100,000 years, but eccentricity — the only orbital parameter with that period — has by far the weakest direct effect on insolation. The cycles are also strongly asymmetric, with slow 90,000-year build-ups and terminations lasting under 10,000 years, which is the signature of a nonlinear system rather than a linear response to forcing. Proposed explanations involve internal thresholds: ice sheets growing until they become unstable through basal melting or isostatic depression, or the carbon cycle amplifying orbital nudges.

The second is the mid-Pleistocene transition. Before about 1.2 million years ago the cycles ran at 41,000 years, matching obliquity, with smaller amplitude. Between roughly 1.2 and 0.7 million years ago they shifted to the longer, larger 100,000-year mode without any corresponding change in orbital behaviour. The leading hypotheses invoke a slow decline in atmospheric carbon dioxide crossing a threshold, or the progressive stripping of regolith beneath the North American ice sheet allowing it to grip bedrock and grow thicker. Neither is settled.

sections.heading: Greenhouse Gases Through Time
sections.body:
Ice cores give the atmospheric composition of the past 800,000 years directly, and the result is one of the cleanest signals in all of Earth science. Across every glacial cycle in that window, carbon dioxide oscillated between roughly 180 parts per million at glacial maxima and 280 to 300 parts per million during interglacials, and methane between about 350 and 700 parts per billion. The oscillations track temperature closely enough that the two curves can be laid over one another and appear almost identical. Before industrialisation, carbon dioxide never exceeded about 300 parts per million in that entire record. It passed 420 parts per million in the 2020s, a level and, more strikingly, a rate of change with no analogue in the ice core archive: the fastest natural rise recorded is roughly 100 parts per million over 5,000 years, whereas the industrial rise has delivered a comparable increase in about 150 years.

The direction of causation during glacial cycles is subtle and frequently misrepresented. At the start of a deglaciation, orbital forcing warms the Southern Ocean; that warming reduces sea ice, shifts the westerly winds, and increases the upwelling of deep water rich in dissolved carbon dioxide, which outgasses. Antarctic temperature and carbon dioxide rise together, with the best current estimates finding no resolvable lag, while global temperature clearly follows carbon dioxide. So carbon dioxide is both an effect of the initial orbital trigger and the amplifier that converts a regional, seasonal insolation change into a global deglaciation. Without that amplification the radiative forcing from orbital changes alone cannot produce the observed 4 to 6 degrees of global cooling at the Last Glacial Maximum; carbon dioxide and ice albedo together supply roughly half the total.

Before the ice core window, carbon dioxide must be estimated by proxy, and the uncertainties are much larger. Boron isotopes in foraminiferal shells respond to seawater pH, which relates to dissolved carbon dioxide, and this is currently the most trusted method. The density of stomata — the breathing pores on fossil leaves — declines as carbon dioxide rises, because a plant needs fewer pores to acquire the same carbon, and this gives independent estimates from terrestrial deposits. Carbon isotopes in alkenones and in soil carbonate nodules provide further constraints, with wide error bars.

The assembled picture for the Cenozoic, the past 66 million years, is a long decline from perhaps 1,000 to 1,500 parts per million in the early Eocene warmth around 50 million years ago to around 280 in the pre-industrial Holocene, punctuated by excursions. Antarctic glaciation began around 34 million years ago as carbon dioxide fell through roughly 700 parts per million; Northern Hemisphere glaciation began around 2.7 million years ago at values near 400. During the mid-Pliocene warm period about 3.2 million years ago, carbon dioxide sat at roughly 350 to 450 parts per million with global temperature 2.5 to 4 degrees above pre-industrial and sea level 10 to 25 metres higher — the closest deep-time analogue to the present, and a sobering one, because the sea level response took millennia to complete.

sections.heading: Deep Time: Hothouses, Icehouses and Catastrophes
sections.body:
Beyond the ice cores, the record becomes coarser but the amplitude of change becomes far larger. The Earth has alternated between icehouse states, in which permanent ice exists at one or both poles, and hothouse or greenhouse states in which it does not. For most of the past 540 million years the planet was warmer than today and ice-free; the present cold state, with ice at both poles, is unusual.

The most extreme episodes are the Cryogenian glaciations between roughly 720 and 635 million years ago, the Sturtian and Marinoan events, popularly known as Snowball Earth. Glacial deposits of that age are found at what paleomagnetic measurements indicate were tropical latitudes, implying ice reached the equator. The mechanism proposed by Joseph Kirschvink and elaborated by Paul Hoffman involves runaway ice-albedo feedback: as ice advances it reflects more sunlight, cooling the planet further, and past roughly 30 degrees latitude the feedback becomes unstoppable. Escape requires volcanic carbon dioxide to accumulate over millions of years, since a frozen ocean and frozen land shut down the silicate weathering that normally removes it, until carbon dioxide reaches perhaps 10 percent of the atmosphere and melts the ice in a violent transition. The distinctive cap carbonates that sit directly on the glacial deposits are read as the product of that aftermath. Whether the ocean froze completely or a narrow equatorial belt of open water survived — the slushball variant — remains genuinely debated.

At the opposite extreme sits the Paleocene–Eocene Thermal Maximum, about 56 million years ago. A carbon isotope excursion of 2.5 to 4 per mil appearing in both marine and terrestrial records worldwide marks the injection of thousands of gigatonnes of isotopically light carbon into the ocean-atmosphere system over a few thousand years.
