Global temperature rose 5 to 8 degrees Celsius, the deep ocean acidified sharply enough to dissolve sea floor carbonate, and benthic foraminifera suffered their largest extinction of the Cenozoic. Candidate sources include methane hydrate destabilisation, volcanic intrusion into organic-rich sediments during the opening of the North Atlantic, and permafrost thaw. The event matters as the closest natural analogue to a large fossil carbon release, though the estimated rate of injection was probably an order of magnitude slower than the present one.

The end-Permian extinction 252 million years ago, the largest in Earth history with perhaps 80 to 90 percent of marine species lost, is now firmly linked to the Siberian Traps eruptions, which released carbon dioxide and sulphur and cooked organic-rich sediments, driving warming of 8 to 10 degrees, ocean anoxia and acidification. The end-Cretaceous event 66 million years ago combined the Chicxulub impact with Deccan Traps volcanism, producing a short, severe impact winter followed by warming.

These deep-time episodes are dated coarsely and reconstructed from fewer proxies, so specific numbers should be treated as estimates with substantial error. What they establish robustly is that carbon release and temperature move together, and that the recovery from a large carbon injection takes 100,000 years or more.

sections.heading: Abrupt Change: The Most Unsettling Discovery
sections.body:
Until the late 1980s the working assumption of most climate science was that the system changes gradually, responding to slow forcing on the timescale of the forcing itself. The Greenland ice cores demolished that assumption, and the result reshaped how climate risk is understood.

What the cores revealed were the Dansgaard–Oeschger events: twenty-five abrupt warmings during the last glacial period, in which Greenland temperature rose by 8 to 16 degrees Celsius in a few decades — in the sharpest cases, layer counting and gas isotope analysis indicate most of the warming happened within one to three decades. Each warming was followed by a few centuries to a couple of millennia of relative warmth, then a slower stepwise cooling back to full glacial conditions. Methane and dust concentrations shifted in lockstep, confirming that the change was not local to Greenland but involved the tropical hydrological cycle and continental aridity across the hemisphere.

Interleaved with these are the Heinrich events, marked in North Atlantic sediments by layers of ice-rafted debris — coarse rock fragments only icebergs could have carried to the deep ocean — signalling armadas of bergs discharged from the Laurentide ice sheet through Hudson Strait. Six such layers punctuate the last glacial, each coinciding with the coldest Greenland phases and a weakened Atlantic overturning.

The physical explanation that fits best involves the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation, the system in which warm salty surface water flows north, cools, sinks in the Nordic and Labrador Seas, and returns south at depth, transporting on the order of a petawatt of heat northward. Freshwater added to the northern North Atlantic — from melting icebergs, from a diverted meltwater river, or from enhanced precipitation — lowers surface density and can suppress the sinking. Model experiments show the circulation has more than one stable state and can flip between them, producing a Northern Hemisphere cooling of several degrees and a compensating Southern Hemisphere warming, the pattern called the bipolar seesaw and confirmed by comparing precisely synchronised Greenland and Antarctic cores.

The Younger Dryas, between about 12,900 and 11,700 years ago, is the best-documented single instance. In the middle of the deglacial warming, Northern Hemisphere climate reverted almost to glacial conditions for 1,200 years, then recovered: Greenland warmed roughly 10 degrees in about 50 years at the end, and the Lake Suigetsu and European varve records show the European vegetation response within a decade or two. The classic trigger hypothesis is a catastrophic release of meltwater from proglacial Lake Agassiz into the North Atlantic, though the routing has proved hard to confirm and alternatives, including a Northern Hemisphere impact event, remain contested and, in the impact case, widely doubted.

The general lesson is not that any particular flip is imminent. It is that the climate system contains thresholds, that crossing one produces change far faster than the forcing that caused it, and that no amount of studying the smooth instrumental record would have revealed this. Monitoring of the Atlantic overturning suggests a likely long-term weakening, but the observational record is short and how close any threshold lies remains genuinely open.

sections.heading: The Holocene and the Last Two Thousand Years
sections.body:
The current interglacial, the Holocene, began about 11,700 years ago and has been remarkably stable compared with the glacial period that preceded it — a stability that almost certainly made settled agriculture and, therefore, civilisation possible. But stable does not mean unchanging, and the Holocene record is where paleoclimatology comes closest to human history.

Early in the epoch, precession placed Northern Hemisphere summer at perihelion, delivering about 8 percent more summer insolation at 30 degrees north than today. The consequence was the African Humid Period, roughly 11,000 to 5,000 years ago, when the West African monsoon penetrated far inland and the Sahara supported lakes, grassland, hippopotamus and human pastoralists — the era recorded in the rock art of Tassili n'Ajjer. Marine cores off the coast of Mauritania show terrigenous dust flux increasing sharply around 5,500 years ago, and the debate over whether the Sahara's desiccation was abrupt or gradual, and how much vegetation-albedo feedback amplified it, remains active.

Northern Hemisphere summer temperatures peaked in the Holocene Thermal Maximum, variously dated between 9,000 and 5,000 years ago depending on region, then declined slowly by perhaps 0.5 to 1 degree until the nineteenth century. This so-called Holocene temperature conundrum is a live disagreement: many proxy reconstructions show the cooling, while climate models forced with known changes in orbit and greenhouse gases produce warming instead. Proposed resolutions include seasonal bias in the proxies, which are dominated by summer-sensitive indicators, and missing processes in the models. It is a good example of a case where the field openly disagrees with itself.

For the last two millennia the density of records is high enough to attempt hemispheric and global reconstructions with annual resolution, combining tree rings, corals, ice cores, speleothems, lake sediments and documentary evidence. The picture that has emerged and been repeatedly reproduced by independent groups using different methods, including the PAGES 2k consortium's networks of several hundred records, shows modest variability of a few tenths of a degree through the Medieval Climate Anomaly around 950 to 1250, a cooler Little Ice Age from roughly 1450 to 1850 with regionally variable timing, and then a sharp, spatially coherent warming in the twentieth and twenty-first centuries that exceeds anything in the reconstructed range.

Two findings deserve emphasis. First, the medieval and Little Ice Age anomalies were not globally synchronous: the warmest fifty-year interval before industrialisation occurred at different times in different regions, whereas the modern warming appears simultaneously almost everywhere, which is a fingerprint of a global forcing rather than internal redistribution. Second, the Little Ice Age is well explained by a cluster of large volcanic eruptions combined with a solar minimum, and volcanic forcing is now recognised as the dominant driver of pre-industrial decadal variability. The eruptions of 1257, 1452, 1600, 1815 and 1883 all appear in tree rings and ice core sulphate, and the year without a summer in 1816 following Tambora is documented in both instruments and harvest records.

sections.heading: Reading a Record in Practice
sections.body:
Understanding how a published paleoclimate record is actually produced and interrogated makes it far easier to judge one, and the workflow is broadly the same whether the material is ice, mud, wood or stone. What follows is the shape of a real project, from field to interpretation, with the decisions that matter at each stage flagged.

Site selection dominates everything downstream. A tree-ring temperature reconstruction needs trees at the cold limit of their range, where warmth rather than water is scarce; a moisture reconstruction needs the opposite. An ice core for gas analysis needs a site that never melts, because meltwater percolation destroys the layering and dissolves soluble gases. A sediment core needs continuous deposition, no slumping, and ideally anoxic bottom water. Getting this wrong cannot be repaired by later analysis.

Recovery must preserve stratigraphic order and orientation. Cores are logged, photographed, split and described before any subsampling, because the visual stratigraphy — a turbidite, an ash layer, a hiatus — is evidence that chemical measurements cannot recover once the material is ground up. Archive halves are kept intact so future methods can be applied to the same material.

Chronology comes before climate. Nothing can be interpreted until an age model exists, and it should rest on as many independent constraints as possible: layer counts, radiocarbon dates on identified terrestrial macrofossils rather than bulk sediment, volcanic tie points, uranium-series ages. That uncertainty propagates into every later statement and should be carried explicitly rather than quoted as a single line.

Only then does proxy measurement begin, and it should include replication — duplicate samples, duplicate cores, blind standards — because drift and contamination are ordinary rather than exotic.
steps: Choose a site where one climate variable is clearly limiting, and document why. Record coordinates, elevation, and the modern climatology of the location.
Recover the material in a way that preserves order and orientation. Mark the top, log depth continuously, and photograph the fresh surface before subsampling.
Describe the stratigraphy visually first: colour, grain size, laminations, ash layers, unconformities, bioturbation. Note anything suggesting a gap or a slump.

Build the age model from independent dating methods. Prefer terrestrial macrofossils for radiocarbon, calibrate with the current IntCal curve, and apply a reservoir correction to any marine or lake carbonate material.
Quantify the age uncertainty as a distribution, not a single number, and carry it through every later plot.
Measure the proxy with replicates and standards. Report the analytical precision separately from the calibration uncertainty.

Calibrate against instrumental data over an overlapping period, then verify on a withheld interval that was not used in fitting. A reconstruction that has never been tested on unseen data should not be trusted.
Compare against at least one independent proxy from the same region with different confounding factors. Investigate disagreements rather than averaging them away.
State the resolution honestly. Bioturbation, layer thickness and sampling interval together set the shortest event the record can resolve; do not interpret features narrower than that.
Archive the raw data, the age model and the code in a public repository so the result can be reproduced.

sections.heading: Failure Modes and How Reconstructions Go Wrong
sections.body:
Paleoclimate reconstructions fail in characteristic ways, and recognising the patterns is the most useful practical skill a reader can acquire.

The commonest failure is a broken chronology. A single misdated tie point can shift a whole section of record by centuries, producing spurious leads and lags between archives that then get interpreted as causal mechanisms. Radiocarbon on bulk sediment rather than identified terrestrial plant fragments is a frequent culprit, because bulk organic matter mixes carbon of many ages, including old carbon eroded from limestone catchments, which can bias an age by more than a thousand years. Marine reservoir corrections that assume a constant 400-year offset are another, since upwelling regions and glacial intervals had substantially larger offsets.

Smoothing and averaging destroy information asymmetrically. Bioturbation in sediment, diffusion of isotopes in ice, and the multi-year integration inherent to some biological proxies all act as low-pass filters, attenuating short events. A record that averages over 300 years cannot show a 50-year event, but it will show a muted, broadened version of it, and comparing such a record to a high-resolution one leads directly to the false conclusion that the past was less variable than the present. The correct treatment is to degrade the high-resolution record to the same effective resolution before comparing.

Calibration failures come in two flavours. Divergence occurs when the empirical relationship between proxy and climate breaks down, most famously in some high-latitude tree-ring density and width chronologies which, after roughly 1960, track observed temperature more weakly than they did earlier in the twentieth century. The causes proposed include drought stress, changing snowmelt timing, reduced solar radiation from aerosol pollution, and artefacts of the standardisation method; no single explanation accounts for all cases, and the problem is site-specific rather than universal. It matters because if a proxy can decouple now, it could have decoupled before. The second flavour is variance loss in regression-based reconstructions: fitting a proxy network to instrumental data by least squares systematically underestimates the amplitude of past variability, because regression shrinks predictions toward the mean. Methods exist to correct this but they must be applied deliberately.

Spatial coverage bias is pervasive. Records cluster in the Northern Hemisphere mid-latitudes, on land, and in the summer season, because that is where trees grow, where ice sheets are drilled, and where scientists work. A hemispheric average built from such a network may be a poor estimate of a true hemispheric average, and the honest response is to quote the reconstruction for what it actually samples.

Finally, there is confirmation bias in interpretation. Wiggle-matching two records by eye and declaring a correlation, tuning a chronology to a hypothesis and then citing the tuned record as evidence for it, or selecting sites after seeing their results are all real, documented practices. The defences are pre-registration of site selection criteria, independent verification intervals, and publishing the records that did not work alongside those that did.

sections.heading: Limits, Open Questions and What the Record Can and Cannot Tell You
sections.body:
It is worth being explicit about the boundary of what this discipline can deliver, because both overstatement and dismissal are common.

What the record establishes with high confidence: that atmospheric carbon dioxide and global temperature have covaried closely for at least 800,000 years and, more coarsely, for tens of millions; that the current concentration and, especially, the current rate of change have no counterpart in that window; that ice sheets and sea level respond strongly to a few degrees of warming, with the Pliocene analogue suggesting 10 to 25 metres of eventual sea level rise at concentrations similar to today's, though over millennia rather than centuries; that the climate system contains thresholds capable of producing regional changes of many degrees within decades; and that the twentieth-century warming is spatially coherent in a way that pre-industrial fluctuations were not.

What remains genuinely uncertain: the exact value of climate sensitivity, which paleo data constrains to roughly 2 to 5 degrees per doubling but cannot pin down because past states differed in continental configuration and ice cover; the cause of the mid-Pleistocene transition and of the 100,000-year cycle; whether Holocene temperatures peaked and declined as proxies suggest or rose as models suggest; how close the Atlantic overturning circulation is to a threshold; and almost every quantitative claim about deep time before the Cenozoic, where dating errors of hundreds of thousands of years and proxy uncertainties of several degrees are normal.

What the record cannot do at all: predict. Paleoclimatology constrains how the system has behaved, which disciplines models and bounds their sensitivity, but the present forcing has no exact past analogue. The rate of carbon release is faster than the Paleocene–Eocene event, the continental arrangement is unlike the Pliocene, and the biosphere is fragmented by land use in a way no past state was. Reasoning from analogy alone is therefore unreliable; the paleo record's proper role is to test physical models that can then be run forward.

For a reader trying to evaluate a claim about past climate, a short checklist serves well. Ask what the proxy physically measures and what else influences it. Ask how the record was dated and what the age uncertainty is. Ask the effective resolution, and whether the claimed event is shorter than it. Ask whether the reconstruction was verified on data withheld from calibration. Ask how many independent archives support the claim, and whether they were selected before or after their results were known. Ask whether error bars are shown, and whether they widen with age as they should. A record that passes all six is worth taking seriously; one that fails several, however striking its graph, is not.

Finally, treat disagreement between records as information rather than embarrassment. When two well-dated archives conflict, one of them is usually recording a real regional difference, and the reconciliation frequently teaches more than either record alone. The field's progress has come largely from taking such conflicts seriously.
